subsubtopic: CRITICISM OF PRAC REPORT ON RAIL LINE ABANDONMENT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a question of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the harsh, crass and insensitive recommendations made by the Prairie Rail Action Committee which suggest 2,280 kilometres of prairie rail lines be abandoned permanently, and since these decisions were made irrespective of any social impact on the communities to be affected and without any consideration of an alternative method of transportation, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil):
That this parliament censor the Minister of Transport for his needless and damaging support of the report by the Prairie Rail Action Committee, a report which contains false and inaccurate comments, and who did so prior to the full and usually impartial consideration of the document by the Canadian Transport Commission.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR MEASURES TO ALLEVIATE SITUATION IN EASTERN CANADA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact the latest quarterly provincial forecasts published by the Conference Board in Canada predict 10.4 per cent unemployment for Prince Edward Island in 1979, 12.9 per cent for New Brunswick, 10.6 per cent for Nova Scotia and 11 per cent for Quebec, and that the Conference Board forecasts show no other provinces in Canada will even approach these high unemployment rates, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Rae):
That the new so-called ministry of development come up with some special projects to alleviate the unconscionable unemployment in Canada's eastern provinces.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ROLLBACK OF BELL CANADA RATE INCREASES- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, to move a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Bell Canada has just announced a very inflationary 37 per cent increase in its profits for 1978, which is the highest return on common shares for this corporation in its history. This has occurred in a year when a rate increase was allowed by the federal government. Because of this terribly inflationary, double-digit increase in profits, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin):
That this government take the necessary steps to roll back the recent rate increases granted to Bell Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED UNAUTHORIZED SPENDING OF PUBLIC MONEYS BY CORPORATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Despite the protracted, strenuous protests of British Columbia members of parliament and thousands of citizens to the construction and development of a second, redundant CBC station within 20 miles of Vancouver, the CBC has gone ahead, constructed the building, ignored a recent cabinet veto of a 1979 broadcast schedule and is preparing right now to begin broadcasting March 31 from Victoria. In view of this situation, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Raines):
That the. government act immediately to halt this unauthorized spending of public moneys against the will of the people and of the executive body of the Government of Canada itself and to halt this repetitive waste of time of MPs and citizens and of taxpayers' dollars in fighting this CRTC-CBC battle over and over again.

subsubtopic: OUTBREAK OF TUBERCULOSIS ON RESERVES IN NEW BRUNSWICK-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In light of the outbreak of tuberculosis on two Indian reserves in New Brunswick-14 known cases and 40 suspected cases-a situation verging on epidemic proportions, and since the Indian Act regulations of 1953 specifically deal with t.b., instructing the federal government to be responsible for prevention and treatment, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this House instruct the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to immediately order the regional director of his department in Amherst, Nova Scotia, to take the necessary steps to stop this outbreak and provide adequate care for those already affected.

subsubtopic: DEVALUATION OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance, who is the first minister of finance in this country for literally some 110 years to have permitted the Canadian dollar to plunge to its lowest average level which occurred in 1978.
Would the Minister of Finance indicate, now that the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. 3ouey, has indicated that a further decline in the dollar would be still more inflationary to the country's economy, whether or not he still believes a floating dollar is a floating dollar?

subsubtopic: DEVALUATION OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext: The answer is yes.

subsubtopic: DEVALUATION OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in line with the minister's little quip, is he aware that international analysts are now saying the Canadian dollar may touch 79 cents this year? Their quip is "79 for 79" in Canada for our dollar. If the minister is aware of this, will he indicate to the House what constructive
January 25, 1979

steps he intends to take to ensure that such a humiliated dollar will not be permitted to occur in this country?

subsubtopic: DEVALUATION OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have stated many times the policy of the government on the exchange rate. I think that what governor Bouey stated yesterday is something with which I am in accord. He is a very competent governor of the bank. I think the hon. member should get busy making sure that on his next trip he does not lose his luggage as he is losing his mind today.

subsubtopic: DEVALUATION OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: DEVALUATION OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can assure the minister that at least I have not lost my credibility, or the value of the Canadian dollar.

subsubtopic: DEVALUATION OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DEVALUATION OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext: If the minister intends to continue his reckless program of borrowing, having expended $5 billion of our reserves in defending what he calls the floating dollar, would he indicate exactly what he means when he states we are now back to a clean float? What is a clean float, bearing in mind that this month alone, especially in the last two days, he has lost another $40 million to $50 million of our reserves defending what he calls the floating dollar?

subsubtopic: DEVALUATION OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext: As long ago as a year and a half I said that the floating dollar is the dollar established by the market. The Bank of Canada has always intervened to make sure there is an orderly market. I hope that some day members of the opposition who like to make a lot of points on this will get up and say if they want us to peg the dollar, and where. They have never had the guts to have any policy on that.

subsubtopic: DEVALUATION OF CANADIAN DOLLAR-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext: Why don't you call on the Governor General?

subtopic: REASON FOR INCREASING RATE OF INFLATION
REASON FOR INCREASING RATE OF INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also to the Minister of Finance and it is on the subject of the Canadian dollar.
Given that it is quite obvious to anybody who follows exchange markets that the value of the currency is highly dependent on price stability in the domestic economy, and considering that the minister has predicted a lessening of inflationary pressures in 1979, can he explain why the advance price indicators-I mention here the industry selling price index and the wholesale price index-continue to show an increased rate of inflation? Where is the underlying trend to lower inflation rates which both he and his predecessor have talked about?

subtopic: REASON FOR INCREASING RATE OF INFLATION
speechtext:
If the hon. member would look at the CPI figures released a few weeks
Oral Questions
ago, he would realize that inflation, which was 9.8 per cent, is now down to 8.4 per cent.

subtopic: REASON FOR INCREASING RATE OF INFLATION
speechtext:
As the minister is well aware, the CPI trails both the indices to which I have referred: both of those show dramatic increases for the latest 12 months' period.
On the question of the dollar, I should like to ask the minister, who has spoken repeatedly-along with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce-about our magnificent trade surplus, the following question. The current account is the determinant of our exchange rate, not the trade position. Does the minister concede that the dollar cannot achieve stability while the current account position continues to increase as it has over the last 12 months?

subtopic: REASON FOR INCREASING RATE OF INFLATION
speechtext: We are working very hard to make sure that the current account is as much in balance as possible. Trade is a very important component, and in fact I am quite sure this year will be a record year for us in trade. However, I should like the hon. member to explain to the House, since he is so preoccupied with balancing the ledger, why his own leader is proposing an even bigger deficit than we have at this time.

subtopic: REASON FOR INCREASING RATE OF INFLATION
speechtext: As the minister knows, a substantial portion of the current account deficit arises from interest payments. The interest payments on the funds that the minister has borrowed and intends to borrow from foreigners will add to that deficit by a considerable amount. Why does the minister think such extensive borrowing is justified now, when it will only lead to a more intractable current account deficit in the future?

subtopic: REASON FOR INCREASING RATE OF INFLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are borrowing abroad at this time because the provinces and the institutions are doing so to a lesser extent than they used to, and thus we are just substituting our borrowing for theirs. Formerly, money was borrowed through intermediaries such as the provinces and companies. However, the level of savings is now such in Canada that most institutional and provincial financing is done within Canada; we are therefore only substituting our loans for theirs on forrign markets. The hon. member should know that Canada always has to import foreign capital because it needs it to develop.

subsubtopic: LISTING OF SUBVERSIVES IN PUBLICATIONS CIRCULATED BY GOVERNMENT

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the 1971 blacklist of 26 individuals which was also circulated by his department, and in view of Mr. Bourne's statement this month that a group would be labelled subversive, and I quote, "if we felt their intentions were contrary to our interests", what guarantees can the minister give that the civil liberties of all Canadians are being protected at this time?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would indicate to the hon. gentlemen that the comments made by Mr. Bourne in that particular context were reflections of Mr. Bourne himself. I would like to review the context within which the comments were made.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT STEPS TO REDUCE OUTFLOW OF CAPITAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, barely a few moments ago, in reply to the question of an hon. member of the official opposition, the Minister of Finance said that we needed foreign capital to develop our country. I totally disagree with that statement. Mr. Speaker, recent reports show that the payment of dividends and interest, which represented a net capital outflow of $4.3 billion in 1977, and $5.5 billion last year will reach, according to various estimates, from $6.6 to $7 billion this year. Can the Minister of Finance confirm those figures? In addition, in view of the disastrous effects that outflow of capital has on the Canadian dollar, does the minis-

ter intend to take specific, efficient and short-term steps to stem that tide?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT STEPS TO REDUCE OUTFLOW OF CAPITAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 am not in a position to give the hon. member a specific answer on the figures he gave, but if he wants to put his question on the order paper, I can see to it that he gets one. As for government policy, we have no intention at this time of imposing controls on foreign exchanges in Canada. We want the flow of money between Canada and other countries to be very free, both into and out of the country, and we feel that it would be untimely at this point, if I fully understand the question of the hon. member, to consider the imposition of foreign exchange controls.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY RESPECTING BORROWING FROM ABROAD
GOVERNMENT POLICY RESPECTING BORROWING FROM ABROAD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
Everybody is aware that the present economic situation in Canada is really bad, and the minister is apparently unwilling to do anything about it. In view of the fact that the government has always favoured borrowing on foreign markets to support the Canadian dollar and that this approach has been unsuccessful and served only to postpone facing the problem of our growing indebtedness, does the minister not feel that this policy ought to be changed because of our extraordinary high level of indebtedness and he should consider a monetary reform as soon as possible?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY RESPECTING BORROWING FROM ABROAD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I feel that if the hon. member would only examine the statistical data closely, he would realize, for instance, that the rate of indebtedness of the Canadian government compared with our gross national product was lower in 1978 than it had been in 1960. Although I am quoting these figures from memory, I think that Canada's debt in 1960 represented 30 per cent of our gross national product, while it represented only 18 or 19 per cent in 1978.

subsubtopic: MINISTER'S VIEWS ON PRAC REPORT ON RAIL LINE ABANDONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Transport. In view of the concern being expressed in the prairies regarding the report of the Prairie Rail Action Committee, can the minister advise if he endorses the report and its recommendations?
January 25, 1979

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: MINISTER'S VIEWS ON PRAC REPORT ON RAIL LINE ABANDONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the action we followed on receiving the report was to examine it to determine whether the positive recommendations seemed supportable, and to act upon those. We have done that. As a result, some further miles of branch lines have been transferred to the basic rail network and now we will be putting in a program for rebuilding.
Some of the recommendations which suggest abandonment are being treated in the same way as the recommendations of the Hall commission were treated in that regard. That means a standover for the Canadian Transport Commission to look at and to be disposed of by that commission.

subsubtopic: MINISTER'S VIEWS ON PRAC REPORT ON RAIL LINE ABANDONMENT
speechtext: In view of the fact that it is not mandatory for the Canadian Transport Commission to hold public hearings with respect to the abandonment of rail lines, will the minister direct the Canadian Transport Commission to hold public hearings in all cases where requests are made by concerned municipalities, towns and organizations?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: MINISTER'S VIEWS ON PRAC REPORT ON RAIL LINE ABANDONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure that I have the power to so direct. However, I am happy to tell the hon. member that the Canadian Transport Commission has already made that kind of decision in an area where certain lines were recommended for abandonment, particularly by the Hall commission and partly by the Prairie Rail Action Committee. Probably what the Canadian Transport Commission has been doing is treating the materials which were fully submitted to the Hall commission as being rather self-supporting for their work, with support from this House because, after all, members on both sides said "Bravo" to the Hall report, "Let it go forward."
Now, as more time has elapsed since the work of the Hall commission, I think the case is made for further examination, with more attention to public viewpoints. I am happy to join the hon. member in drawing this fact to the attention of the Canadian Transport Commission through this forum.

subtopic: SUGGESTION PRAC WENT BEYOND TERMS OF REFERENCE
SUGGESTION PRAC WENT BEYOND TERMS OF REFERENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the same minister, on the same subject. In view of the very close relationship the minister has had with the hon. member for Assiniboia, particularly with regard to presenting goverment positions to this House, and in view of the fact the hon. member for Assiniboia stated last Friday that the Prairie Rail Action Committee report went beyond its terms of reference, will the minister advise whether the hon. member for Assiniboia was speaking for the government when he made that statement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: SUGGESTION PRAC WENT BEYOND TERMS OF REFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not seen that statement. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre has just claimed across the House that he made that statement. I want to determine whether they were both saying the same thing before making any further comment on that matter.
Oral Questions

subtopic: SUGGESTION PRAC WENT BEYOND TERMS OF REFERENCE
speechtext:
Just to refresh the minister's mind on this matter, 11 months ago, on February 28, speaking for the government on that occasion, the hon. member for Assiniboia said the Prairie Rail Action Committee had three urgent tasks: the first was to recommend additional, immediate transfers of lines from the suggested prairie rail authority category to the permanent network in order to facilitate the building of grain companies, and so on. That was honestly a government statement. He has now come out a year later and said that this report by the Prairie Rail Action Committee repudiates the Hall commission report and recommends the abandonment of an additional 1,400 miles of line which Hall recommended belongs to the authority of the Prairie Rail Action Committee.
Obviously, my question is whether the minister is now repudiating the statement made by the hon. member for Assiniboia a year ago when he was speaking for the government and laying down to the House the policy and the purpose of the Prairie Rail Action Committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: SUGGESTION PRAC WENT BEYOND TERMS OF REFERENCE
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, I certainly am not. I rebut the argument by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain that the Prairie Rail Action Committee was in any way in conflict with the Hall commission. It is true that the Hall commission left a great number of lines in doubt. That is a point which hon. members opposite like to gloss over. The Hall commission did not say how long those lines were going to remain.
All the elevator companies, including the pools, came to us immediately and said that that continued period of doubt was going to be very serious, because they would not know whether to construct facilities on the lines in doubt or larger facilities on the neighbouring lines which were certain, and they wanted these issues resolved. Accordingly, we appointed the Prairie Rail Action Committee to continue the work of determining which lines should remain and which lines should be referred to the Canadian Transport Commission for further examination by that commission.
This is precisely the approach which the Hall commission used in regard to the lines before it and it left in doubt a certain category having resolved the issues in regard to the other categories. This work, therefore, was continuing to provide certainty. Of course, where the real certainty comes is in the rebuilding program, because not only are we declaring certain lines to be there and permanent, but we are rebuilding them with many millions of dollars and that is what is really going to make for a good transportation system on the prairies.

REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON USE OF INFORMATION CONCERNING SUBVERSIVE ELEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Solicitor General and it relates to the documents known as "The Whizzer" and "The Special", and the publicity attaching to them recently.
Acknowledging that most, if not all, democratic countries make use of documents of this nature in terms of identification of individuals or groups presumed to be engaged in subversive activity, but acknowledging also that that use is restrained by the need for accuracy of information within a document, by the extent of circulation of the document and by the use to which the information is put by its recipients, will the Solicitor General take this opportunity, or undertake to give a statement at an early date as to the use to which the information contained in these two documents is put by its recipients?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON USE OF INFORMATION CONCERNING SUBVERSIVE ELEMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. gentleman that all countries have systems whereby information is exchanged. That is essential if we are to protect ourselves internally, as we do in Canada, from subversive activities.
As the hon. gentleman knows, the Weekly Internal Security Service Report which has been referred to is prepared by a branch within my department, the police and security branch, in order to permit various security heads within departments to be mindful of activities which chould be interpreted as being dangerous and threatening to our internal security. I can assure the hon. gentleman that the distribution of "The Whizzer", the Weekly Internal Security Service Report, is very limited and is only for the purposes envisaged under section 16(2) of the Official Secrets Act.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON USE OF INFORMATION CONCERNING SUBVERSIVE ELEMENTS

Will the Solicitor General be more definite in terms of circulation? Without wanting to know the names of the individuals on the circulation list, 1 ask the minister whether he can tell us, or undertake to make a statement at least in general terms as to the number circulated and the general nature of the recipients who are on the circulation list.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. My understanding is that the Minister of Transport made a statement about a Canadian merchant fleet and the refusal of this government to have anything to do with a Canadian merchant fleet.
In making that announcement, I wonder whether the minister took into account or discussed with his colleagues, particularly the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the feasibility of offering meaningful tax concessions to those who might be interested in putting together the capital necessary for the creation of such a fleet.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: INCENTIVES FOR CREATION OF MERCHANT MARINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter of the exact nature of our shipping policy was fully discussed within the government and it was decided not to move with major tax incentives or other forms of support at this particular point in time. However, I think it should be pointed out that a good deal else was done with regard to our shipping policy and we remain convinced that it is best for our shippers and our major exporters and importers to have available world shipping at the lowest possible rates.
January 25, 1979

We are taking steps to protect ourselves against various world arrangements which might tend to work to our disadvantage, and we are also arranging to protect the Arctic for Canadian shipping in a way which should assist entrepreneurs in Canada to move ahead into the field of shipping and to be in a position to move forward with even more effort in the future.

subsubtopic: INCENTIVES FOR CREATION OF MERCHANT MARINE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, aside altogether from the apparent contradiction between what the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce just said and what the Minister of Transport is now saying, that a shipping policy is in place, I wonder whether the Minister of Transport is aware that in failing to consider this course of tax concessions, he not only fails to evaluate the gains for Canada in terms of employment, not only in construction and in manning but also in the fact that he and this government are condemning Canada to adding at least several hundred million dollars to the already unfavourable balance of payments.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: INCENTIVES FOR CREATION OF MERCHANT MARINE
speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, a good deal of the examination has gone into the question of service to particular elevators since the time of the statement by the Prime Minister.
In looking at the question, the Hall commission knew, on one hand, that elevator companies would not willingly indicate that they would give up service on any particular line but, on the other hand, many times they made it clear that they were required to significantly give up service in particular areas and cut back in the number of remaining elevators.
Obviously, at that point the Hall commission recognized that they could not let one elevator company keep a couple of elevators on one line and the other company keep a couple on the other line, when comparable service to farmers could be provided by those elevators being rearranged in a different way. Hence, the Hall commission reached certain conclusions about lines to be abandoned and lines to be retained.
The Prairie Rail Action Committee has been continuing this work with an eye on the over-all cost of rebuilding the lines. The point is that unless the lines are rebuilt, they will die and it is not just a matter of keeping the lines but a matter of rebuilding them. This is very expensive and it has to be looked at seriously, and I think that that is the process we have engaged upon.
I say again to the hon. member and the elevator companies that if they have a particular case to make, they can be assured of the opportunity still to make that case to the Canadian Transport Commission. That is where the next decision point lies.

subsubtopic: TABLING OF TASK FORCE REPORT "A FUTURE TOGETHER"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to table in both official languages the report of the task force on Canadian unity entitled "A Future Together", along with its observations and recommendations.
This report is a landmark contribution to the collective search by Canadians for a more harmonious and secure relationship between our linguistic, regional and cultural com-

January 25, 1979
National Unity
munities. I am confident the report will take its place as a document of the first importance, and it is a source of great satisfaction to me that the report should be the product of an initiative taken by this government.

Our creation of the task force took its place alongside our other initiatives to advance Canadian unity and the renewal of our federation. The report comes after intensive negotiations between the federal and provincial governments, and at a time when we are about to hold a second first ministers' conference on the constitution. It can only reinforce the urgency which our government and several of the provincial governments have attached to constitutional reform. While the commissioners recognize the profound and urgent character of the crisis of Canadian unity, they have written a report marked by the optimism and even serenity arising from their faith in the immense value of Canada for all its people. The wisdom of the commissioners is evident in their ability, arising from a strong will and a spirit of compromise, to submit a unanimous report. This is all the more remarkable given the comprehensive scope of the task force's analysis and the short period which it had to complete its work.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that we in this country and in this House should express deepest appreciation to the co-chairmen, Mr. Jean-Luc Pepin and Mr. John Robarts, to the other commissioners, to the staff of the task force, and to all those Canadians who contributed to the report.

I am sure that all members of the House, all members of the provincial legislatures, and many thousands of Canadians will want to read and reflect carefully on this report. Given the nature and urgency of our present crisis, I believe we should try to use this report to improve our understanding of the nature of our problems and to seek as much agreement as possible on the principles and methods of their solution. Individual passages or recommendations in the report will give rise to some disagreement, but I believe it is incumbent on us to try first to understand the over-all analysis and principles of the report before we take issue with this or that specific point. We will find a solution to our national crisis only through a wise spirit of accommodation. My plea is all the more important because the report is so remarkably well integrated, with its different elements depending closely on one another.
Although the government for its part will want to study the specific recommendations carefully and take issue with some of them, I can tell the House now that the government accepts the broad lines of the task force's analysis of the problem and endorses the basic principles which it believes should underlie the renewal of the Canadian federation.
[ Translation]
First, the report is clearly federalist in its orientation and it advocates the entrenchment of basic rights in our constitution. Thus it is consistent with the two essential pre-conditions

which this government has advanced for renewal. The commissioners' commitment to federalism in the Canadian context comes as a conclusion to its analysis of the nature of Canada and of the principles which should govern our relationships.
The commissioners deeply believe that federalism, better than any alternative, is sufficiently consistent with the realities of Canada and the aspirations of Canadians. What is more, they state their conviction that any proposal to create a new arrangement with an independent Quebec joined in some sort of association with the rest of Canada would be inconsistent with the realities of the country and therefore unacceptable and unworkable.
Second, the report bases its analysis on the intricate structure of Canada: a structure which combines both a multifaceted dualism, and a complex regionalism.
Third, the commissioners set forth three objectives for Canadians which I am sure will receive wide support and which recall the government's own position set out in "A Time for Action." These objectives are, and I quote:
-to treat diversity as a national resource rather than a social problem;
-to encourage greater sensitivity to the Canadian dimension of our lives; and -to seek to understand as well as possible the major forces operating on Canadian society and to develop public policies and institutions on the basis of that understanding.
Finally, I must admit to taking special satisfaction from the way in which the commissioners have largely supported the official language policies of the government and their recognition of the great gains these have produced. I am quick to acknowledge that this policy was largely supported on both sides of this House, Mr. Speaker, and I hope the report of the task force will ensure that the Official Languages Act continues to receive broad, non-partisan support.
I will stop here. This day belongs to the members of the task force and the thousands of Canadians who contributed to their report.

speechtext:
This task force is important in what it is and it is important in what it has done. It is a group of authoritative Canadians who do not have vested interest to protect, except a vested interest in the continuation of this country, and who are reporting to us today after extensive and direct consultations with the people of Canada.
What the task force has done is to propose several specific changes, some of which will be highly controversial here and certainly some of which will be highly controversial in the other place. The great service is that in this debate it has moved us above specifics to reflect the widespread belief that exists in Canada that some significant and fundamental changes are necessary if we are to maintain and preserve this nation.

As is known, Mr. Speaker, as leader of a national party I have had many opportunities to travel across the province of Quebec and to discuss with Quebeckers about possible changes in the nature of the society of a federalist country. I often noticed that for most Quebeckers it was not enough to speak only about specific changes, about detailed changes as in the case of culture and communications. What people seek in Quebec as well as in Alberta is an indication of a will to consider somewhat more deeply such changes that can help keep together the federal system and at the same time contribute to the well-being of Quebeckers and other citizens across Canada.
National Unity

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I think it is very important that we move from a stage where we have been perhaps too occupied with details and recognize that there is, not simply among elected officials, among commissioners and task force members, but among the Canadians this task force has been consulting, a very real determination to contemplate some significant changes in the form of our federal nation in Canada.
One thing that it is very important for us all to recognize as we look at this report is that there are a number of matters which will require detailed discussion and which will ignite some significant disagreement in this chamber and in the country. I do not think it is appropriate to enter into that detailed discussion at this time, but I think it is worth drawing attention to some aspects of the report which are particularly important.
I am struck by the fact that for virtually the first time in a decade we have an extensive work done by an authoritative group on the serious and fundamental problem of the division of power in this country. Indeed, I think it is fair to say that this document reflects the first major study of the direction that a new distribution of power might take.
I think a very valuable contribution of the task force is the emphasis that has been placed, properly and importantly, on the need for improved co-operation among governments at federal and provincial levels to ensure that our economic policies are integrated and are moving forward together.
Again, I think it very valuable for the debate that is in progress in this nation that we have from the task force their recognition and description of the provinces of Canada as the principal vehicles of regional expression, including, and perhaps particularly including, the province of Quebec.
I think it is very important for us in this House to consider very seriously the changes that have been proposed in some of the national institutions, including to consider with an open mind some of the changes that have been proposed for the means of composition of this particular parliament. Those specific proposals put forward by the task force have been very helpful. Other proposals will lead to very serious concern in some parts of the country, particularly those relating to the rights and status of minority language groups in various provinces, and will require further discussion here and elsewhere.
It is important that we acknowledge that the road toward a strong and united nation requires a recognition that we are engaged here in a process. It requires, as the task force members pointed out, a much greater understanding of our country by Canadians. Each of us comes simply from one corner of it; we need to give much more attention than we have to means of getting Canadians to travel across the country, to make them more informed about regions other than their own. It clearly requires a high investment in tolerance and understanding in this country. It means that we have to build upon

January 25, 1979
National Unity
the successes we have had-and we have had some successes. But it means that we have to be prepared to put aside preconceptions that have not worked.
I would like to say at this time, Mr. Speaker, that I think we have followed for too long the pretence that a language policy or an amending formula or any other single act would unite this country, or indeed that a referendum or any other single act would destroy this country. So life is not as simple as theory is.
The task force report confirms the view that for some time now the constitutional policy of the central government has been dramatically out of step with reality in this country. Of course, some of the government's initiatives have been valuable, and the task force quite properly applauds, for example, the progress that has been made in easing and encouraging the access of Francophone Canadians to the services of, and to significant roles within, the national government.
But if individual programs have seen some success the general pattern of the decade since our centennial has been for the people and the parts of this country to move in one direction and the central government to move in the opposite direction. The stark conclusion of the work of the task force is devastating. I quote from page 35 of the English version:
One of the principal sources of the crisis is the erosion of the belief that the current arrangements of the country promote the common good.
Sir, what is important for parliament to recognize is that it is not simply a case of some of the current arrangements becoming out-moded, although that has happened; it is also that some of the new arrangements imposed by this government go against the grain of the country. This government has resisted regional aspirations when they should have embraced those aspirations. They have concentrated political power when some of that power should have been dispersed. They have been so preoccupied by their intellectual view of what Canada should be that they have ignored what this nation is.

We are very much a country to grow in. [Translation]
And I think that there is a statement in this report which must be emphasized. It is to the effect that Quebeckers are now less concerned about their survival and more about their development. That is a very significant change in attitude. They have moved from a negative to a positive approach. More than ever Quebeckers feel proud and sure of themselves. And I am convinced that most Quebeckers are aware that a new Canada would facilitate their development which I feel is of paramount importance to all Canadians.
Reforms are necessary, but the best spring board to achieve this development of the Quebec people is a country filled with opportunities, and Canada is such a country.

The first ministers are meeting again in constitutional conference in a few days. I would certainly hope that if it fits their agenda it will be possible for them to consider the report that has been put down by the Task Force on Canadian Unity. But I also hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will indicate his willingness today to refer this report to the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution of Canada that has been established by this House and by the other place so that it will be possible for the House of Commons, which is the central legislative agency of this country, and the Senate to carry on discussion of some of the very important new dimensions that have been given to this debate by the report which we have been honoured to receive in this parliament today.

speechtext:
As has already been indicated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark), the commissioners have taken a serious and comprehensive look at the problem of national unity, recognizing it has very complex economic, social and political dimensions. The commission has ably explained our heritage and our difficulty in language that Canadians can clearly understand. But importantly Mr. Speaker, they have provided Canadians with an opportunity to look at our complex situation in a very positive context.

The report of the task force certainly contains precise recommendations, but it is mostly with a wide open approach that it indicates the way to build a new Canada and ensure
January 25, 1979

national unity. The task force strongly affirms its commitment to federalism. It also emphasizes that the uniqueness of Quebec's culture may be preserved and fully developed within a united Canada. We agree with that statement.

The report shows that Canadians throughout our various regions, and not simply in Quebec, have legitimate grievances with both the present structure of federalism and with the ongoing nature of government policies. It has proposed a number of workable solutions to these grievances. I find it refreshing that the task force recognizes the problem of national unity is not simply a constitutional matter and that the development of the national economy for the benefit of all Canadians in all parts of the country is a crucial element in keeping us united.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
The commission recognizes the necessity for an industrial strategy, and makes it clear, contrary to some of the reports that have appeared in the press, that to achieve this there can be no substitute for the federal government having the major economic power in this country. This is a point which I have been stressing for many months and I welcome the report's clarity in this regard.
As for some of the specific proposals and recommendations contained in their report, I want simply to say that there are a great many which are positive and beneficial as well as some, as should be expected, which ultimately a number of us will have to disagree with. In terms of the positive ones, I think particularly of the highly imaginative and constructive approach it has taken in recommending a list of several categories of powers to be distributed between the federal and provincial governments. I repeat, this is one of the most imaginative and constructive parts of the report and requires the most serious consideration by members on both sides of this House as well as the provincial governments.
I think also of the acceptance of the proposal I made on behalf of my party to strengthen regional input in Ottawa by adding additional members to the House of Commons on a proportional representation basis from the provinces.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
In the days between now and the first ministers' conference, my colleagues and I will be studying the report very carefully indeed. I will therefore refrain at this point from making any further comments on specific recommendations of the commission. I want, however, this afternoon to draw particular attention to the framework for constitutional reform suggested by the commission because I think it is singularly appropriate.
At one point in its report the commission lays out three objectives of constitutional change. They are as follows. First, to ensure that our central institutions can effectively serve our common interests as a nation. Second, to provide means of
National Unity
greater institutional responsiveness to regional and provincial desires for more effective local control and for a more effective influence on decisions that are to be made and ought to be made in Ottawa. Third, to provide for the majority of Quebe-cois an effective federal means of ensuring that their distinctive cultural and social ideals can not only be maintained, but can flourish.
I speak on behalf of my colleagues, and I suspect in this context on behalf of all members of the House, when I say that those of us who have the heavy responsibility-and it is heavy-for acting and voting on these matters could not work from within a better framework in dealing with the constitutional aspects of national unity than that provided for us by this commission. I repeat my thanks.
I want to conclude my remarks this afternoon by stressing that constitutions can provide a nation only with a framework. No constitution, however good, ever held a nation together. A country as complex and as rich as ours, in particular, can work only if its politicians make the right policy decisions and convey the right set of attitudes over a period of time.
The question of continuing political leadership in the broadest sense is therefore crucial to any federal state. In our own day, I cannot overemphasize the relevance of economic policy on the one hand, and an honest, Canadian nationalism recognizing what the commission has called our duality on the other. As I said in a debate on this subject which took place in parliament a year ago, we as politicians should be noting with pride the remarkable creative accomplishments by French and English speaking Canadians, particularly, but by no means exclusively, during the past two decades.
Simultaneously, we should at long last be charting a course in which Canadians would gain economic control of our country. In short, given the proper constitution, we politicians must convince Canadians in Atlantic Canada, Quebec and the west that we as a people, can create a country that is both just and exciting. Ultimately, it is that which holds a nation together.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the commission on Canadian harmony, as I would call it, has tabled its report. Since I have just skimmed through it, I cannot voice an enlightening opinion on its substance. Even the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) expressed reservations in his statement because he had not had time to read it entirely and ponder over it. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that all my colleagues will realize that I am entirely justified in making this point clear.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this report comes in just at the right time because a federal-provincial conference likely to determine the future of our country will be held in February. This is why I urge all members to study this report carefully because it was prepared following investigations and hearings held across the entire country. As the right hon. Prime Minis-

January 25, 1979
National Unity
ter put it eloquently, the commissioners have succeeded in presenting a unanimous report even if they were of different views. Some of them had reservations about certain points but they overcame this in their desire to present a unanimous front to help the federal and provincial governments work out a new constitution.
Mr. Speaker, in the name of my party, I also wish to thank the members of the task force who have done a very commendable job and who had to work many evenings to table a report that will serve as a guide to the federal government, the Canadian parliament, as well as the provincial governments of our country.
Mr. Speaker, I would like that a copy of this document be made available to all Canadians so that they could realize the seriousness of the situation and be sufficiently informed when the time comes to take a final decision to accept or reject a new constitution which would guide our country in a future of harmony and progress.
Mr. Speaker, when I was a schoolboy and saw a large colour painting of the fathers of confederation, I was impressed by the solemnity of their faces and the magnificence of their clothes. I could feel these Canadians had worked to give our country a constitution we could be proud of and which would enable us to live in harmony on our land, and that both English and French-speaking Canadians would share this land, secure from the quarrels that divide us and make us unhappy. Today, in the statements that have just been made by the spokesmen for the various parties, I heard the word "Quebec" which kept cropping up in their vocabulary. Well, Mr. Speaker, I for one would not like you to be concerned about Quebec owing to the possibility of a government who wants to hold a referendum to decide whether Quebec will remain in the confederation or not.
Mr. Speaker, our nation is a more serious reality than that. We must, and that is our responsibility, give our country a new constitution. It has been long enough since we started discussing whether or not we are going to repatriate the 1867 constitution. And I believe, and I already said so in the House at the time of the debate on the right hon. Prime Minister's motion in July 1978, that it is important for us to give our country a new constitution. I ,made proposals at that time concerning the way the new constitution should be prepared, either by the public, or by our civic groups, by all serious organizations in our country, as long as they are not political groups, which would be able to submit consistent views in order to help our politicians in their efforts to draft a new constitution which would give any Canadian equal chances, regardless of his language, religion or province of origin.
And I am convinced of one thing, Mr. Speaker, that is every province in our country wants self-determination. I can see here in the task force's report a passage which roused my curiosity earlier today, a very meaningful passage, at page 74

of the English version, in the chapter entitled "The Quebec economy and federation." What did the commissioners say?
Quebec's dissatisfaction with Confederation goes beyond economic considerations. It is rooted in the Canadian federal system which in the eyes of Quebecois has somehow failed to give Quebec the desired degree of political autonomy in several important policy areas. While the issues are exceedingly complex they largely revolve around political matters such as the distribution of powers.
In that respect all governments in Canada, whatever their political colours, must plead guilty. We have to admit that openly because the constitution of 1867 was not applied to the letter and the central power in many cases took away from the provinces the areas of jurisdiction that presented provincial governments from fully exercising their responsibilities with respect to their subjects. I am not blaming anyone here, I am merely stating a fact, and the commissioners continue to want that. And yet, in the debate surrounding the possibility of seeing Quebec separate from the rest of Canada, economic questions play a large role.
Mr. Speaker, if economic questions play a large role, we must include financial questions. I am sorry, I read again in yesterday's La Presse that the government of Quebec was going to borrow another $150 million in the United States. Mr. Speaker, as long-and here I urge the right hon. Prime Minister to think seriously about this-as the Parliament of Canada and the government do not take the responsibilities so that the matter of the creation of the money supply in this country is not the responsibility of chartered banks but the responsibility of the government through the Bank of Canada, we are going to have problems of that nature. Canadian harmony will not be possible because the various governments go beg abroad the permission to develop our natural resources for the benefit of Canadians. I am sorry that the commissioners-at least I did not see it-did not deal with that aspect of the problem that divides Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude by commenting on what the Prime Minister said in his statement earlier. He insisted on the objectives set out by the task force on page 4 of considering that diversity as a national resource and not a social problem. On that I agree, we cannot all be the same. There are as many diversities as there are individuals. There are as many diversities as there are cultures. And in spite of that, it could be possible to live in harmony if we used the means to make us more mutually harmonious, to understand one another better and have equal opportunity to live decently right across this country, whether it be in Newfoundland or Vancouver, Quebec city or New Brunswick. That must be provided in a new constitution, and I for one, as a Canadian, am prepared to make the necessary efforts and to encourage greater sensitivity to the Canadian dimension of our lives as it is said at page 4 in the Prime Minister's statement. I agree with that but it should not be only empty words.
We will have to act, we must show courage, and our policies should not be dictated by financiers who are growing ever

January 25, 1979

richer at the expense of the government, at the expense of the poor. That situation must come to an end and this is the only way to have harmony in Canada. I am prepared to co-operate with the Prime Minister and with parliament. We should stop praising each other, we should tell the truth. We must now suggest means and solutions. Many times people have laughed at Social Credit members and their financial options. That was called "funny money", but considering what our dollar is worth today it is no longer funny.
Everyone bows before international finance. This has gone on long enough. It is time to stand up straight. Let us show that we are proud people who can take our responsibilities, that this parliament, its 264 members, its Prime Minister and ministers are able to take their responsibilities, and we shall see that there will be harmony in our country whatever our age, our religion, and our linguistic policy may be.
The Prime Minister has made enormous efforts. There have been resignations in his cabinet. However, these efforts must continue because it is essential that, from the east to the west and the north to the south of our country, each Canadian who wishes to speak English or French can do so with dignity without being embarrassed and that each Canadian can communicate with the Canadian government institutions in the language of his choice. I am not ashamed to say so, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). As the Prime Minister knows, the Task Force on Canadian Unity travelled extensively in Canada and heard many views. I know something about those views because I participated at the meeting in Winnipeg and made a presentation to the task force, but the report that we have before us today in many respects does not reflect the view of the
National Unity
Canadian people which I heard expressed not only in Winnipeg but in other places. On the other hand, it seems to follow very closely the pattern of the old Bill C-60 which was before the House and "A Time for Action" to which the Prime Minister himself referred a few moments ago.
My question to the Prime Minister is whether he believes that this report which we have before us today is a reflection of the will of the people of Canada, or is it just a reflection of a few hand-picked members of the task force?

speechtext: I ask the Prime Minister in all sincerity, through you, Mr. Speaker, is he hearing from the people or is he hearing from a few members of the task force who are echoing his own words?

Mr. Speaker, I will point out to the hon. member that the task force was not just composed of a few members but was made up of a large group of Canadians from all walks of life and all parts of Canada, and they spoke with one unanimous voice. I think it is demeaning to them to suggest that they are merely echoing the government's policies. If the hon. member were to address himself to some of the recommendations, he would see that there are some divergencies, some honest ones.
As to whether or not they speak for the people of Canada, I think they did their best to reflect remedies which would be good for Canada. That is not to say that all Canadians are aware of what those remedies are. I think the hon. member is an illustrious example of one member who does not seem to be aware of what is necessary to keep Canada united now.
As to who speaks for Canada, I imagine no one speaks for Canada more than the parties in the House, and the four leaders of the parties have said that generally they support the task force report. So it would seem to me that the hon. member is rather in a minority in suggesting that this report is not important and does not correspond to the needs of Canada at this time.
