speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to spend a few moments participating in this debate in two capacities: first, as the very proud representative of the largest fishing constituency in all of North America, not merely in Canada, on the south coast of Newfoundland; and also as Secretary of State for External Affairs, where the impact of the 200-mile limit, in which I am very pleased to have played a part, is a major matter of concern and indeed already some satisfaction for me.
In the amount of time available obviously it will not be possible to touch on all matters I would like to deal with in this particular debate. However, with the indulgence of the House, I will attempt to answer a number of questions which were raised from time to time, and also to give my views reflecting conversations which I have had with fishing interests in eastern Canada over many years.
January 25, 1979

Hon. members will understand and appreciate that I will be speaking principally about Newfoundland fishery matters, but that much of what I have to say applies with equal weight to all of the Atlantic fishing area. In the first place, this debate, as well as other discussions which have taken place over the years and in recent months in the House, have been extremely productive and have revealed that on fundamental questions there is a high level of agreement about fishery prospects. Now we can look to the future of the fishing industry with much more confidence and optimism than at any time in the past.
It would be a mistake to argue that there are no longer differences of view, but such differences as there are, some of which are substantial, have been revealed in discussions between members on this side of the House and members opposite, and even in discussions between members opposite themselves. The differences have more to do with methods and timing of expansion, but, most importantly, with where the economic control will lie in terms of the future expanded fishery to which we have referred.
One of the most useful results of the intensive talks was the demolition of a number of hardy and persistent myths about the fishery and the revelation that much conventional wisdom needs to be challenged vigorously. Today I hope to be able to challenge some of that conventional wisdom, not only as it is uttered from time to time here, but, perhaps more importantly, as ii is uttered by pseudo experts on the outside who would probably not know a dory from a prairie schooner if they were hit on the heads with the two of them at the same time.
There are two basic questions which are central to the current discussions: first, what is the nature and potential of the fisheries resource; and second, what is the best manner to exploit it to achieve maximum benefits for Newfoundland, Newfoundlanders and, by implication, all Canadians?
It is evident from the statistics and the detailed discussions in many fora that while the 200-mile limit and various conservation measures have been of great help, as well as various things which the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) introduced, the fishery stock situation has now turned around. To use a familiar expression, we have bottomed out. I think the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment would be the first one to agree with me.
There will not be a dramatic overnight recovery. Even with good management practices, it will take from five to ten years to rebuild the stocks of most species that are or are likely to be important to eastern Canada. This gradual, orderly build-up is, in my view, a good thing. It will permit the expansion of the fishery to proceed in a well organized, coherent way on the three important and integrated fronts of catching, processing and marketing. Clearly, all three must be kept in phase, and there is recognition on all sides now, I believe, that our markets are not sufficiently diversified and are in a more precarious state than is generally realized.
I could spend a great deal of time deflating some of the myths that I have referred to which seem to suggest that the
Government Organization
market situation is now one of being essentially a seller situation and that we can do virtually whatever we wish. My day to day experiences as Secretary of State for External Affairs make it perfectly clear to me that the road to better markets in the future is by no means wide open to us as yet, and that we must take a number of very careful steps if we are not to set back another decade or more the very useful, forward motion that has been introduced in the last couple of years.
We must therefore avoid being carried away by grandiose schemes and over-optimistic, exotic solutions, even though these may be appealing and on first utterance may seem to provide many of the answers. I believe it is essential that we examine all proposals for fishery development carefully and with the greatest degree of hard-nosed realism.
We must recognize, for example, that by itself the fishery cannot answer all of the economic problems of Atlantic Canada, but particularly of Newfoundland, and cannot be everywhere the employer of last resort, even if our best expectations for the industry are realized. Nevertheless, fishery development along modern lines is the best economic generator Newfoundland can have.
I have a few reasons for saying that which I would like to explain to hon. members. First, the fishery is a resource-based industry, and a renewable resource at that. Second, many aspects of the fishery are labour-intensive and therefore tremendously important in an area of high unemployment. Third, the fishery is a widely dispersed industry geographically; and fourth, a fishery-generated dollar stays in Newfoundland longer, and thus circulates more frequently among many more Newfoundlanders. I would venture to bet that it could be demonstrated by economists that a fishery dollar in the Atlantic provinces is infinitely more valuable-perhaps by three, four or five times-than any other dollar generated, let us say, from secondary industry or from some other source.
There is another overriding reason for the special place and importance of the fishery in Newfoundland. It is part of the social fabric of the province and the main supporter of a distinctive lifestyle. Whatever other elements are added, the Newfoundland fishery must be the key and foundation for any development strategy. Having reached this inescapable conclusion, we must then address ourselves to the basic question of how fisheries development should proceed.
I would like at this moment, Mr. Speaker, to express my congratulations to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment and my admiration for him for the very thorough and solid approach which he has taken to fisheries development in eastern Canada and in the country at large. I do not believe that even the most vehement partisan in the country could possibly argue against the very clear and concise manner in which he has proceeded. Certainly, there are very few fishermen in Newfoundland who are likely to be in any way contradictory in their assessments and their views. By the same token, I think it is also to the minister's credit that he has resisted some of the grandiose plans to which I have referred and that he has been so patient in seeking to examine all of the

January 25, 1979
Government Organization
ramifications of various proposals that are put forward. It is eminently sensible for us now, for the first time in Newfoundland's 450 years of history, to say that we are going to take this revived resource and use it properly, something which we probably have not done since John Cabot made his first report in 1497 "that you could catch fish in a basket weighted with stones". From that day on, there has never been a coherent fisheries policy in eastern Canada, and the minister is starting now to put one together.
One of the myths which I consider has been laid to rest is that there are essentially two fisheries. All of my life, growing up in fishing villages on the coast of Newfoundland, I have heard people talk about the two fisheries as if they were indeed water-tight compartments, if you could have water-tight compartments in the fisheries context. They are described as the inshore and the offshore or deep sea fisheries.
This is a long-standing and widely-held misconception. The fact is that how the offshore fishery is managed determines the fate of the inshore fishery, and thus the fate of thousands of inshore fishermen. If too many fish are caught offshore, then there will not be enough for the inshore fishermen; if you limit the offshore catches to revive the stocks, then the inshore fisheries flourish. It is a simple, straightforward equation, and it puzzles me why it is so difficult to get the fundamentals of that statement through the heads of many people involved in the fishing industry in Canada.
It must be emphasized, of course, that the inshore and the offshore fisheries are not mutually exclusive. It is not just a question of saying that if you have the inshore you can have the offshore, and it is not a matter of having one or the other. It is very much a question of balance, and in considering what that balance should be, I believe there is now unanimous agreement-certainly there is agreement between myself and the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment, and perhaps in fisheries terms that has some relevance and importance-that the inshore fishery comes first. The primary objective and the first task is to build up the opportunities and the livelihoods of Newfoundland's existing inshore fishermen and to make it attractive for many others to enter this fishery around the province, but particularly for those who are familiar with the geography along the northeast coast.
Since this is the goal without which no fishery strategy can be successful, it therefore follows that policies on fleet development-our over-all catching capability-are of crucial importance, far too important for us to allow the development to take place helter-skelter or for us to encourage some individual enterprise, no matter how well meaning, that might very well be out of phase with the comprehensive plan which must have as its central goal the protection of that huge number of inshore fishermen in our province and throughout eastern Canada.
There is no serious shortage of catching capability at present in the Newfoundland fishery. This is another of the myths which I wish I could explode, and I hope that I will have the

opportunity of doing so today, at least for those who are particularly interested.
I would emphasize once again that my constituency, ranges along close to 900 miles of coastline and it has approximately 20 of the largest fish plants in North America and some of the most skilled fishermen to be found anywhere, whose livelihood is studied by people from all over the world seeking to improve the lot of their fishermen. Therefore, I believe that my sources are impeccable, and I would take them by a long shot over theories of those people who, in good will and with all manner of initiative, would undertake separate enterprises.
When I talk to my constituents, these fishermen, who, by the way, are among the few in eastern Canada or Newfoundland who are on the grounds now in mid-winter, who have a most difficult lifestyle and deserve my respect and my attention, their message to me up and down the coast is that there really is not a serious shortage of catching capability at the present time, inshore or offshore.
There are some special problems, Mr. Speaker, and these are areas that require attention. As decent-minded and fair-minded people anywhere will acknowledge, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment has not been rigid and we have moved to take care of some of these special problems. In the case of the deep sea fishery, there are areas where particular plants have not been well served, and through the minister we have made accommodations to them.
In the case of the deep sea fishery generally, however, all the stern trawlers-now the majority of the offshore fleet-are still operating at catch rates considerably below capacity. I believe that this is an important consideration for us, but not merely in the context of the offshore. If I can translate this into the larger issue of an industrial strategy for Canada, this is a classic example, in minuscule, of what we mean when we talk about optimizing our productive capability.
This fleet of vessels by and large is underutilized, and therefore we must ensure that instead of bringing in half loads or three-quarters on a trip over ten or twelve days, these vessels are maximized to bring in full loads, perhaps in a shorter time. Faster turnarounds would make sure that the vessels are maximized in terms of their capability of contributing to the general well-being of the industry. That is what the minister and governments, both federal and provincial, must look at. This is not because in some particular or other an entrepreneur may wish to add to the fleet in a specific way; rather the question is whether the totality of the catch capability is being utilized to the maximum extent.
As for the inshore fishery, Mr. Speaker, many fishermen are turning away from the more expensive boats. This is a fascinating phenomenon and the wise, experienced fishermen in Newfoundland for years have been telling me it was going to happen.
If I may be critical of the theorists and indeed of some of the minister's bureaucrats-I am sure he will not be offended
January 25, 1979

by this-there was a period when big was considered beautiful in fisheries terms.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) may not be referring to my physique when he talks about big being beautiful. He is beautiful, whether big or little,
I can assure him.
In this context let me say that here is a prime example of the failure over many years to understand that the fishermen knew best. In many cases we were telling them: "You are not really as well off as you think you are because you ought to have a bigger boat, you ought to have a more complex operation." The result was that much policy-federal, provincial and private-was aimed in that particular direction. I repeat, these larger, more expensive boats are being questioned now and the fishermen are preferring smaller fishing units with smaller crews, less overhead and carrying charges, for the simple reason that they wind up with more money in their pockets at the end of the day.
When we talk in developmental terms about expansion, growth and things of this nature, I think we must always bear in mind the very germane lesson of the fishermen. You can have a fisherman as industrious as any get out with a 300-foot boat capable of being used for a variety of purposes, which costs a minimum amount of money but has modern gear, is equipped with radar and safety features. With one assistant he is going to do very well. If instead of a 30-foot boat he gets a 60-foot boat, then he has a crew of four or five people, he is paying off a mortgage no matter how generous the terms, he has added fuel costs and a whole range of other things. Although it looks great, the harbour is "cheeched" from one end to the other with large vessels. His profit is actually smaller than when he was dealing, as we say, cross-handed or with one or two people aboard with him.
In these talks about fisheries, Mr. Speaker, I have always a tendency to lapse into the vernacular. If some of the words do not convey themselves in either official language to the interpreter, I apologize.
There is much more I could say on the subject but I want to move on. Based on the fundamental assumption that the inshore fishery must be put in a healthy condition, it can be concluded-I have already concluded and am prepared to defend my conclusion anywhere before any audience at any time-that the provision of an adequate mix of inshore fishing vessels able to meet all anticipated needs is not an insurmountable or even serious problem provided all parties work together to devise practical programs of financing, orderly expansion and, of great importance, catch disposal. What I am seeking to convey is the idea that it is wrong to look through the small end of the telescope and see the problem as bein', of such proportions that it is simply not capable of being managed.
Just taking a figure out of the air, if you have 5,000 inshore fishermen at a cost per boat of $40,000 or $50,000, you say that is a massive challenge. If you turn the telescope around, however, and realize it is a whole series of small, individual,
Government Organization
personal enterprises and deal with it in that fashion, and if the minister continues his humane and personal kinds of policies of sitting down with individual fishermen and groups of fishermen, then you do not have to talk in multi-million dollar terms.
Indeed, people in Newfoundland and in my riding would be perfectly happy if they were able to go to somebody and say, "I need $30,000 or $40,000. How do I go about getting it and what is the best arrangement?" If I have a criticism-which I have-of the bureaucratic structures that this government and every other government tends to create, it is that there is too little disposition to be attentive to the small entrepreneur who is not interested in becoming, and does not need a massive bureaucratic machine in order to become, self-supporting and perfectly content to be able to get off unemployment insurance or anything else that might be offered to him as an alternative.
I think it is important to recall again the linkage between the inshore and offshore fisheries. The greater the percentage of stocks assigned to inshore, the less complex the task of determining the size and make-up of necessary offshore fleets.
I want to make it clear, as anyone who has any association with fisheries will understand and agree, that what I have said about the inshore fishery does not mean that we cannot and must not have a most effective, most efficient, most modern offshore catching capability. What I am getting at and what I emphasize once again is that this mix and the emphasis put on the inshore fishery is going to determine the kind of fleet needed for offshore development. It is only possible to get this mix properly when you see the two in the same context. I realize I am getting into too much detail here for this particular audience.
This leads to another basic developmental proposition. The offshore vessel acquisition program must place the emphasis on the gradual replacement of the present fleet. The need is not for large numbers of additional vessels now; indeed, if there was a cornucopia of funds available, whether in the private sector or through governmental largesse, the answer for us on the east coast today is not suddenly to double the size of the offshore fishing fleet. What we need now is a sound, rational program which puts into place a clear picture of what the fishing fleet consists of at the present time-how old the vessels are, what is the point at which they start to become obsolete and less efficient-and then to put mechanisms in place, both public and private, so that new and modern vessels are phased in and therefore we increase our catching capability to synchronize with an increase in the stocks available. That is something which is terribly important and which will require the intricate co-operation of federal and provincial governments, fisheries representatives, the unions and everybody concerned.
By the way, I should add here that we also need to have a much better awareness than is universally held at this time about how we get at presently unexploited species. We have had a rather narrow range in terms of all of the various species

January 25, 1979
Government Organization
of fish in the Atlantic that have been attracted to Canadian processors or even to Canadian fishermen. I think we are on the road to this, but obviously there will be disageements; I have no difficulty with that. It is a question, however, of taking all of the parties concerned and discussing the matters in detail. With good will, I think we can work it out.
I want to emphasize this gradualness of the replacement program for the same reason that I talked about the inshore, and that is to counteract the erroneous impression-and it is very, very erroneous-that there is a massive and immediate need for a huge fleet of new, sophisticated offshore vessels. Perhaps those who are landlocked Canadians may welcome an explanation, if altogether too brief a one, of the costs involved. If we go to a new catching capability which will engage 10 or 12 fishermen at sea, the cost is in the many millions of dollars. That same expenditure, if it were put into inshore facilities, would engage many hundreds of persons. The relevant economics are very complex and have to be worked out so as to ensure that one does not get too large an increase in production capacity inshore.
At the same time one does not put all of the money into what is, in the absence of the proper balance, very much a high expenditure item in terms of fish fleet, capital cost in the first instance, and maintenance beyond that.
Whatever disagreements exist on this issue of fisheries-and I believe down underneath there are very few, but I repeat what I said at the beginning-there are differences of emphasis and differences of approaches, and for something as complex as the fisheries one could not really expect that not to be the case. But on the question of catching capacity there is no dispute whatever, so far as I have been able to see. I hope hon. members will understand that what I am seeking to do here is to demystify some of the frequent and repeated comments that one hears that are really not grounded in fact.
This basic conclusion which is so fundamental to what we are talking about is that in terms of conventional fish plants Newfoundland, and probably all of Atlantic Canada, have more than enough facilities, far more than enough facilities right now. So that once again when we speak of exploiting the 200-mile limit, it is not then a question of saying we are going to bring a large number of fish ashore-I have already demonstrated this is in itself a complex question-but also of saying that we must build a whole new massive infrastructure in order to look after it.
That is simply not the case. Virtually all of the plants that we have now are underutilized and their productivity is affected adversely. Some of them in seasonal areas are operating at 20 per cent, 30 per cent, or 35 per cent capacity, maybe a few even less, yet we continue to hear many reports of fishermen having to dump their catches at certain peak seasons and of some plants being unable to obtain extra ships to process additional supplies. This is a real dichotomy, a tremendous contradiction, and yet one that has so far defied some of the most intense planning that people have put into it. What we must do is to in a sense marry the supplies side to the

production side, and many good steps have been taken in that direction.
I want to emphasize here that the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment has been very forthcoming in terms of the amount of federal assistance provided through his department, through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and in a variety of other ways in co-operative undertakings with the provinces, in this case Newfoundland. I believe we have been moving at an accelerated rate toward this rationalization which is essentially what is so important for the future.
There is one point I want to make again, and I realize in talking about this subject that there are not many more than the Minister of Fisheries, myself and perhaps oui friend from the Magdalen Islands who will really understand what I am speaking about, and I hope they will forgive me for not going into more detail in the interest of saving time. One of the valuable things to emerge from the recent discussions has been to remove the curse, as it were, from that much maligned historical fishery which we refer to in Newfoundland and in Atlantic Canada as the trap fishery. For years claims have been heard that the trap fishery was a nuisance; too much small fish, the annual "glut" problem of catches too big in too short a time, and the wastefulness of dumped, unsaleable catches.
The tendency has been to "think around" the trap fishery, to contemplate its phase down or even its abandonment, and to consider it a nuisance to orderly planning. I do not know that there is an analogy in farming that I might use, but it is as though one had a crop that was 50 per cent of the value of the year's yield, but it was a bit of a nuisance and you kept saying to yourself: "How can I get rid of this particular crop?". It took us in our case maybe 450 years to realize that it is fundamental to what we are doing in fisheries on the east coast.
The fact is that without the trap fishery there simply cannot be a viable inshore fishery. The trap remains the most efficient catching method yet devised in inshore terms, and well over 50 per cent of the cod landings come from traps during the relatively short season. In brief, an effective inshore strategy must be built around the trap fishery. It must be the centrepiece and not, as it has been for centuries, an undesirable fringe.
I want to conclude with one or two important comments about the 200-mile limit and its ramifications. This is more in the context of my responsibilities as Secretary of State for External Affairs, although clearly there is an interface between that and my responsibilities as the member for the riding of Burin-Burgeo, soon to be Burin-St. George's. All of this new activity and new opportunities offered have been a result of the acquisition of the 200-mile limit. Few subjects can generate more enthusiasm these days. But let me caution the House that the misconceptions are legion also. These centre on all aspects of foreign participation, from quotas to joint ventures and non-Canadian ownership of processing facilities in Canada.

I:

January 25, 1979

It is becoming increasingly apparent that with only a lapse of two years this month since the declaration of the zone it is still too early for a consensus to emerge or for sound, longterm judgments to be made on some very fundamental questions. There are some known facts and others are now emerging after a period of just 24 months. The over-all picture is starting to clarify and we are learning what the choices are before us.
I think that it is of the utmost importance that we recognize that one cannot correct the abuses of literally centuries in two years. Nor is it possible in two years to get a total perspective on what new circumstances are to the point where one can put in place regulations or policies which are inscribed on tablets of stone and are incapable of being changed.
To start with the fundamentals, Canada now has exclusive fisheries jurisdiction out to a distance of 200 miles. The legal status of this jurisdiction in international terms is complex, but for practical purposes it can be said-and I want to say it this way-that Canada has first claim on all fish stocks in the designated region. Strictly speaking, Canada is not obliged to consult any other country on how it will manage the zone or on what disposition it makes of any of the living resources the zone contains. It is a very simple and straight forward proposition. Nevertheless, one question that has been raised repeatedly is, why not bar all foreign activity from the Canadian zone, in effect establish "a fence" 200 miles around the Newfoundland coast and keep all but Canadians out?
I want to deal with this point. It is I believe one of the misunderstandings that must be disposed of if we are to have effective future planning for fisheries. In time it could come to this point, that for policy reasons or otherwise we might be able to build this kind of fence. However, as things stand at the moment, there are a number of reasons why it is not wise to do so at the present time. Among these is the fact that there are some species within the zone that Canada does not take at present or where we cannot take all that is available. I believe this is an important consideration. The objective is to gain concessions for Canada from other countries by assigning the quota surplus, and I emphasize the word surplus, to Canada's needs on an interim basis. Such concessions include easier and wider access for our Newfoundland fish products for the countries in question, particularly Europe. Also, as I was able to demonstrate over the Christmas holiday, some of the concessions that we can obtain are, for instance, the ability to have some 60 odd Soviet fishing trawlers repaired and overhauled in our Newfoundland dockyards as a result of this 200-mile arrangement. All of these are matters which certainly argue for some degree of flexibility on the 200-mile zone.
I could spend a lot of time talking on many other aspects of the fence question, but I want to emphasize one in particular, and that is, as has often been said, that the fish will not know where the fence is. That is probably the most important consideration of all when it comes to answering the question why we do not bar everybody from 200 miles inward.

There are large quantities of fish-I believe the figure has been estimated in the order of 25 to 30 per cent of some species, certainly 20 per cent-that are actually outside the 200-mile area. These, of course, could be ravished. This would have a very detrimental effect if we did not have international agreement and understanding as to how those stocks were going to be dealt with.
We have the makings of that in the new organization which came into place on the first of this year, the successor organization to ICNAF, the International Commission for the North Atlantic Fisheries. I believe we are taking wise steps under the guidance of the Minister of Fisheries.
There was much more I wanted to say, but I think I have taken too much of the time of the House already.
I do want to make one final point. In all of the talk now going on about joint ventures and the like, rapid expansion and special new kinds of arrangements for fisheries, there is a real danger that both Canadians and foreigners may overestimate the degree of co-operation possible in the foreseeable future. The hard reality, not yet fully recognized, is that for most of the species in which foreigners are interested there is no surplus. This is something which has escaped a lot of people who talk in a rather airy-fairy fashion about fast expansion or rapid growth. It is quite the contrary. We are still short for our own immediate needs and the requirements of conservation and replenishment.
Put very starkly, the present opportunities for foreign cooperation are decidedly limited and, in this sense, the issue of joint ventures of various kinds is being grossly exaggerated in some quarters. This does not mean that opportunities are non-existent. It simply means we must look at them very carefully in each individual case where they arise. If we do that, we will form a pattern or rationale which will turn out in the end to be most beneficial as far as we in Canada are concerned.
These are the sum of the reservations expressed to me by many people, including, most importantly, all of the people for whom I have the greatest respect, namely the fishermen. They are not asking us to move into massive, astronomical kinds of expansion. They are not saying to us we are going too slowly. They are not saying we should be having big deals here, there and the other place, and all sorts of consortia and the like.
Many people in Newfoundland remember at least three major companies, all of them by coincidence in my constituency, which moved in the last time there appeared to be marvellous opportunities but which were not at all hesitant to turn the key as soon as things turned down. I can assure hon. members that memories are long about those kinds of experiences.
There are many more specific issues relating to fishery development on which at some point there should be the opportunity for detailed discussion in this House and elsewhere. In my mind, the union in Newfoundland is properly- and I have been supportive of this-stressing the key role of

If this can be done, there is no doubt that to Newfoundland the fishery is more than just another industry. Mr. Speaker, I feel compelled to pay tribute to the eloquence of the previous speaker, who spoke about the romance of the fishery. I have never experienced that romance. I want to speak about the romance of another industry which is connected to this reorganization which we are speaking about today.
It has been said that there are nutritional qualities in fish that help the brain. I assume that must be true. I am, however, compelled to think that other things that are said about Newfoundlanders must be true as well, because I have been reading the speeches made in defence of the fishing industry in 1971 when fisheries became a minor department under the new Department of the Environment. It has often been said

that Newfoundlanders put the cart before the horse. I really wonder about the mess the fishing industry has been in all these years when those members have been in power and have had the direction over that important industry.
The latest attempts at government reorganization remind me of something a recognized member of the forestry industry said recently. He said that he does not get any great feeling of optimism that we are really making progress; that while things are being changed, he is not sure they are being improved. This bill is not an attempt to make government more efficient but an admission that previous attempts to reorganize, particularly in this area, have failed. This is nothing new.
Since the emergence into this arena in 1968 of the intellectual giant and social engineer there have been attempts to reorganize all kinds of things. My colleague the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) enumerated the government programs which have been the subject of attempts at change, but there has been recognition that some changes were wrong, and we have had to go back to where we started from.
I want to say just a little bit about one department which was changed about the same time that fisheries and forestry came under the Department of the Environment in 1971, namely, the department dealing with the Unemployment Insurance Commission and manpower. There was a separation there, and it took eight years before hon. members opposite recognized that mistake and that the problem of manpower management in our country is much better handled under one department. Now we are undergoing the painful process of reamalgamating those two departments at great cost to the taxpayer and at great human cost to the public servants we have asked to undertake these reforms.
Fisheries was an autonomous department of government until 1971, when the Department of the Environment was formed. What we see today is a return to an original policy, namely, a fisheries department like the department which was formed by a Conservative government and which had a high profile until the new administration came along.
My submission, however, does not concern the new ministry of fisheries as much as it does the remaining Department of the Environment, such as it is, and the component in that department which is known as forestry. In general terms I support the objectives of the bill and my colleagues on this side of the House support those objectives; but for the life of me I cannot understand why the equally crucial problems relating to forestry are once again ignored.
As hon. members know, there are three major areas of jurisdiction under the Ministry of Fisheries and the Environment. The third major area is forestry. I would like to review how the former department of forestry, like fisheries, has been reformed to death. Before 1968 the forestry department was a separate and autonomous department of the federal government. In 1960 it was known as the department of forestry and from 1966 to 1967 as the department of forestry and rural development. In 1969 forestry became a branch within the
January 25, 1979

department of fisheries and forestry. It became a service known as the Canadian Forestry Service within the newly created Department of the Environment in 1971. The reorganization of the Department of the Environment in 1974 downgraded the Canadian Forestry Service to a relatively minor role in a massive department which by its nature is oriented more toward environmental protection than toward the enhancement of the economic values of our forest resources.
At the moment the federal government is in a poor position to co-ordinate provincial forestry programs because there is not even a deputy minister who is able to advise the environment minister on matters relating to forestry. Dr. Place, director of the program development branch of forestry, appeared before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry where he made the following statement:
-owing to divided jurisdiction, Canada does not have a clearly enunciated national forest policy. This is an area in which our Department would like to take some initiative in trying to promote more of a consensus in the future but it is a typical area because, not only is there divided federal and provincial jurisdiction, there are some 20 agencies within the federal government having their finger in the forestry pie and no single department has a clear mandate to see that federal activities are co-ordinated.
This is the present state of affairs as it relates to the once proud Canadian Forestry Service and, indeed, as it relates to this very important component of the industrial capacity of this country. It should be added that just in the last few weeks the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has driven the final nail into the coffin by his decision to deprive the Canadian Forestry Service of what little was left to it to sustain some very important, vital and crucial research efforts. We have heard much in the House in the last few days and weeks about the reorganization of the Petawawa forestry research labs. As hon. members know, it was decided to phase that service out. Then after we brought the concerns of the industry and the professions into the House, the minister and the government decided that instead of phasing out the station it should be reorganized and that the Forest Management Institute, the Forest Fire Institute and the services connected with them should be transferred to Petawawa. The minister is probably quite right when he says that there will be more bureaucrats at Petawawa than there were before, but the services have been drastically reduced.
I wish to take this opportunity to provide a profile of the forest industry. I want to speak in defence of that industry, which has been the backbone of our economy for longer than any of us can remember. It has been the backdrop to a social environment which is indispensable to many Canadians. The Canadian Institute of Foresters had this to say in its policy statement:
The forest lands of Canada, including associated wildlands, provide an environment basic to the economic, social and spiritual well-being of Canadians. They are vital in providing raw materials for the wood-converting industries, in maintaining a quality fishery and wildlife habitat, in purifying air and water, in regulating water supplies and in making available to Canadians and to their visitors a vast outdoors in which a multitude of recreational, educational and scientific activities can be carried out.

TRANSFER OF QUEEN MARY VETERANS HOSPITAL Mr. Hal Herbert (Vaudreuil) moved:
That an humble address be presented to His Excellency praying that he will cause to be laid before this House copies of all correspondence, notes, minutes of meetings, agreements and other communications between the government and the province of Quebec concerning the transfer of the Queen Mary Veterans hospital in Montreal.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have risen in the House many times to speak about the transfer of this hospital, the Queen Mary Veterans Hospital in Montreal, and the transfer of other
2568

Transfer of Veterans Hospital
hospitals, as well as on the subject generally of veterans and veterans' care. I spoke specifically on the subject of this transfer some five years ago. I have expressed my concern and received assurances from the minister that the veterans would be properly looked after.
I have no doubt, and certainly I have no evidence to the contrary at present, that the veterans who were sick in the hospital have not been well treated. What does concern me is that, in my opinion, there is not free access to documents. By dint of placing many questions on the order paper I have received answers, but the answers are not necessarily consistent.
In October of 1977 the minister issued a news release in which he stated the following:
Under the terms of the transfer agreement-
That is an agreement to transfer the Queen Mary Veterans Hospital to the government of the province of Quebec.
-entitled veterans will have priority access to 55 acute care beds in Montreal hospitals. Further, the staff of the hospital will become employees of the new hospital corporation under terms and conditions of employment similar to those they enjoy in the federal public service ... The effective date of the transfer is December 26, 1977, when the Department of Veterans Affairs will transfer for one dollar the grounds, buildings and equipment of Queen Mary Hospital to the Quebec government. The province will also receive from the Government of Canada an indexed capital grant of $9 million for reconstruction purposes.
That is basically it. It is just about all we know about the transfer. We are advised that whenever a veteran requires admission for examination, treatment or care, that veteran, when beds are not fully occupied by veterans, will be admitted without delay.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) stated the following yesterday in answer to a question:
Beds guaranteed to veterans under the transfer agreements specified are: ...
(f) Queen Mary Hospital, Montreal-55 beds.
In the same answer he recounts that on January 1, 1978, at the same Queen Mary Hospital there were 260 patients who were receiving acute care treatment. Six months later, on July 1, 1978, that number of veterans had dropped to seven. They are all listed as acute care cases. Thus it would appear that we have a signed agreement giving veterans access to 55 beds, and from the reply of the minister given as late as yesterday a much smaller number of veterans occupying those beds. He does not give a more up to date figure than that of October, 1978 when the previous figure of seven to which I have referred dropped to five.
What concerns me, of course, is that in my constituency of Vaudreuil we have another veterans' hospital, the Ste. Anne de Bellevue Military Hospital, with something in the order of
1,000	patients and a long waiting list. Since for some time there has been a long waiting list, and since the number of veterans who are likely to be requesting admission in the next few years is likely to increase because of their age, there would appear to be a need for even more beds for veterans than are presently available. Nevertheless, from the figures which are presented to us, having passed the Queen Mary Hospital over to the province, we have not only reduced the number of

veterans receiving a federal level of treatment from some 260 to something in the order of about five, but we are not using anything like the total number of beds, that is 55 beds, that we have reserved for veterans at the Queen Mary Veterans Hospital.
I am also told-and this maybe will be worth recording for the benefit of those who, like myself, until a few days ago were not aware-that the agreement signed with the province provides that Canada will retain at no rental charge no less than 66,249 square feet of usable space. I was interested in what we were to do with the space and was told that the departmental treatment services are going to use 21,000 square feet of space. This is all for the Department of Veterans Affairs. The departmental dental services will use 1,508 square feet and the prosthetic workshop of the Department of National Health and Welfare, 5,000 square feet. Then I also see that we have retained space for chapels and chaplains' offices amounting to 2,172 square feet. This is fairly decent accommodation for the personnel and for the chapel for the five remaining veterans in the Queen Mary Hospital. We also retained some 14,620 square feet for departmental veterans' services, for veterans' land administration 6,641, for the Canadian Pension Commission 4,879 square feet, for the bureau of pensions advocates 4,100 square feet, and for the departmental central registry 6,329 square feet. The total is 66,249 square feet, as I mentioned before.
In other words, all these federal facilities are still continuing at the Queen Mary Hospital, formerly the Queen Mary Veterans Hospital. I sometimes wonder whether the veterans who formerly used these facilities are still aware of their continuing use.
I am also advised-here I am somewhat concerned and I should refer back to an answer I received from the Minister of Veterans Affairs on December 7, 1977-that when Queen Mary Veterans Hospital was transferred, some of the medical records of the veterans were maintained in the hospital and others were transferred to the Public Archives record centre in Montreal. Also the minister indicated that in the future those medical records which no longer need to be maintained in the hospital will be transferred to the record centre. He indicated in his reply that the medical records to be maintained in the hospital would be the records of those veterans who were continuing to receive treatment at the hospital. That would be quite logical. However, it appears the agreement provided that Canada shall transfer to the province all medical records in connection with each veteran. Of course, that raises some questions. Some of the veterans in my area have asked me if they will have the same access to their records as previously.
I have asked the Minister of Veterans Affairs questions in connection with veterans' records. I am pleased by the manner in which these records are kept, and the fact that veterans can go back to their wartime service and find records were kept by the department of which they were not even aware. Also I compliment the department in that it freely discloses what is on the records, thus enabling veterans, in many instances,

successfully to claim various pension benefits which, without the department's records, they may not have been able to obtain. It underlines my fears that a department which has done such an excellent job of maintaining medical records of veterans apparently is prepared to turn over these records to the province of Quebec. I am concerned because of the attitude of the present government of that province, its general attitude toward anything which could be termed federal. Also I am concerned that veterans will not continue to have the same access to medical records as previously.
I am interested in what the terms of this transfer are, as well as the discussions which have some bearing on the transfer of this particular hospital. In March, 1977 I suggested that there was a problem at the Ste. Anne de Bellevue Veterans Hospital because we were unaware whether the hospital was going to be transferred, when it would be transferred, or what the conditions of the transfer would be. I realize the problems of disposing of the Ste. Anne de Bellevue Veterans Hospital.
On April 7, 1975 the minister indicated that less than 20 per cent of the patients in Ste. Anne de Bellevue Veterans Hospital were considered to be a federal responsibility. Also he indicated that the province was only paying for part of the costs of some 524 patients out of a total 804 patients who were considered to be a provincial responsibility. In the balance of his answer, he indicated that in other words the provincial government was paying 28 per cent of the total operating cost of the hospital, while more than four out of five veterans occupying beds in the hospital were considered to be a provincial responsibility.
That is one reason why I doubted the transfer would ever be effected. Obviously it would cost the province of Quebec a considerable sum of money, and the province would have to accept the responsibility for patients who were not directly a cost to the federal government. I expressed my opinion that some of the fears of the patients and the staff at the Ste. Anne de Bellevue Veterans Hospital could be allayed if they were made aware of the precise conditions under which any transfer would be made.
One way in which we can be assured that the federal government will look after veterans is to look at its past history. In order to do that, we wanted to look at all of the records in connection with the transfer of Queen Mary Veterans Hospital. Also we noted the sum of $9 million which was handed over to the provincial government for renovations at the Queen Mary Veterans Hospital. It was interesting to note that the subject came up in connection with the Senneville Lodge which is part of the total facility at Ste. Anne de Bellevue Veterans Hospital.

At the present moment it is not intended that the Senneville Lodge property which comprises the main acreage of the Ste. Anne's complex will be included in the transfer although the patients at Senneville Lodge will be looked after by the hospital authorities after

transfer until such time as a replacement unit of the nursing home type is built at federal expense, probably in close proximity to the main hospital.
That was fairly reassuring for the patients at Senneville Lodge. On November 10, 1976 the minister indicated that planning for the replacement of the Senneville Lodge in Quebec was deferred while discussion was continuing with the province of Quebec respecting the transfer of Queen Mary
Veterans Hospital. Also he said that when these discussions were completed, the department would undertake definitive planning for the replacement of the Senneville Lodge. I was somewhat puzzled that these two matters would be tied together, but I accepted it at that time.

However, the site has not yet been determined and the plans for the replacement are not finalized. It is evident that there are connections between Senneville Lodge and the Queen Mary Veterans Hospital for reasons unknown. One should be able to reassure persons by openness to rid veterans of most of their fears. The hon. member has also pointed out that many veterans may not be aware of the use of transferred hospitals. This is an issue I have raised before. Lately we have had some serious problems with regard to veterans gaining admittance to veterans' hospitals. There have been two deaths. One of the deaths occurred because the individual was refused at the Sunnybrook Hospital in Toronto. This particular veteran had difficulty gaining admittance to the hospital which had no available beds, and he was therefore refused. He was left on a stretcher in the emergency ward for more than three hours and then sent back to the Centenary Hospital. Shortly after he was sent to St. Michael's Hospital for surgery where he died there the next day.
There is a similar case which occurred in Victoria recently. The minister has stated, in referring to the veteran's wife, that she did not properly apply to get into the hospital. This was a concern expressed by the hon. member for Vaudreuil, that he was not sure whether or not veterans or their families knew how to apply for admittance to these hospitals.

He made no specific reference to the recent veterans who died because they were shuffled from hospital to hospital. I will pursue this matter at a later date, because we are just not satisfied on this side of the House.
The hon. member for Vaudreuil has stated that the veterans have not been made aware of the system. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to address myself to the motion put forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert). He has asked that the minister table all correspondence, notes, minutes of meetings and other communications between the Government of Canada and the province of Quebec having to do with the transfer of the Queen Mary Veterans Hospital.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) has asked that there not be any partisan politics. At least the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs over the past years have been above partisan politics. I would therefore hope that the critic for the opposition will continue in that vein and not simply point out some of the shortcomings of the Liberal party. He knows full well that we on this side of the House have the well-being of veterans at heart, as I am sure all members do in this House.
As I understand it, the reason that the hon. member for Vaudreuil wants the information about the minutes and the contracts is so that the people in his riding and in St. Anne de Bellevue hospital may know the terms of the agreement and the contract being transferred. I suggest that in all cases where we have transferred these hospitals there has been an equitable agreement or arrangement made and that the people working

January 25, 1979

in them have not suffered financially, any loss of position, or in any other way.
As Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) I have visited the hospitals which have been transferred from the Government of Canada to the provinces. I was in Victoria where there was some problem in the beginning, which has been cleared up. In talking to the people concerned, I found all of them quite happy with the way things have been handled and how they now stand. In Edmonton we have been in negotiation for the transfer of the veterans hospital there. I have visited Edmonton and I am sure that matter will turn out as well as the transfer of the Queen Mary hospital in Quebec.
It has been suggested that we would talk out the motion, Mr. Speaker. I do not know about other members, but I am here because I have a few points to make about the transfer of the Queen Mary hospital and other transfers, and so that I may share with my colleagues and the people of Canada what the Department of Veterans Affairs has been doing, is doing, and will continue to do for the betterment and good care of the veterans who are our responsibility.
I think the most important statement I can make is that the government recognizes and accepts its moral responsibility to provide the best possible medical care for our veterans. That is where we began, and I am sure that no one in this House and no one in Canada would disagree with the concept. There are sometimes misconceptions about the way the government provides this medical care. I am always glad to have a chance to correct those misconceptions.
It is now more than 30 years since the end of World War II and in that period the most dramatic changes have taken place in the field of medical and hospital services, hospital care and administration. Most significant to the question at hand in the medical and hospital field is veterans population. To appreciate what is happening now to the hospital care and treatment of veterans we need to look at what has happened in the past and in the intervening years.
When World War II ended and the injured troops were returned to Canada, the existing hospital facilities were totally inadequate for their accommodation. To provide the needed beds and treatment, the government had to build hospitals specifically for veterans. At one time there were 40 veterans' hospitals in Canada. The war injured were most in need of acute care. The vast majority needed it only for a limited period of time, and most were discharged within a period of months.
My colleague, the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton), served as a surgeon in World War II. He has worked in veterans' hospitals, and I was talking to him about this prior to today's debate. This private members' hour, incidentally, should not be called the period of futility, in my view. It is a time when members get a chance to bring up subjects that are important to them and their constituents. My colleague assured me that the care given to the returning veterans from World War II in those hospitals where he served was second to none anywhere on the North American continent.
Transfer of Veterans Hospital As the damages of war were repaired and the patients recovered, some of these hospitals were closed down within a relatively short period of time. They had been built in response to a special and abnormal health care requirement, and as that requirement was met, progressively the hospitals closed and we were left with a few hospitals where veterans received medical care for pensionable disabilities. Over the years the number of veterans requiring acute and active care steadily decreased, and as beds became empty they were made available to DVA recipients.
Slowly but surely the profile of the veteran patient changed. In the beginning there were young men severely wounded and needing the most immediate, sophisticated medical treatment possible. That immediate need was taken care of. The veteran patient's need became one of periodic hospitalization and treatment later on for pensionable disability.
With the passage of time the veteran population aged and its needs changed again. Most of the beds in veterans hospitals were filled with people in need of care for chronic conditions and frequently these were of a geriatric nature. In terms of our ability to staff these hospitals, this meant we began to have serious problems. Highly skilled young doctors and nurses trained in the most modern medical procedures are not prepared to work in hospitals where they get little or no opportunity to use their skills or perfect their skills and become better at their chosen profession. It is understandable that they want to work in hospitals where they can gain experience in the widest possible range of medical practice.
The practice of medicine today is incredibly specialized and every day it is becoming more so. The modern hospital has specialists available for virtually all the ills to which mankind is heir. Veterans' hospitals do not have the volume of patients to justify equipping and staffing them to meet the full range of medical treatments. This gap between what we can provide and what is needed will increase in the future as the health facilities of communities continue to improve. I am talking now about the medical complexes which are in place across this land where these men and women, who are veterans of World Wars I and II and the Korean war, can receive the specialized care they not only need but deserve. We could see this situation on the horizon. We knew the care of veterans had to be integrated into the total community medical hospital complex. To do anything less would be to deny our moral responsibility to continue providing veterans with the best medical care possible.
When negotiating contracts with provincial governments to transfer hospitals to provincial jurisdictions, the policy of the government is to provide only the best in medical care. This is what we have done and what we are doing and will continue to do in the months and years ahead. This is why we negotiated the transfer of the Queen Mary hospital with the province of Quebec. This is why I do not doubt that in the foreseeable future we will begin negotiations with other hospitals in other parts of Canada-so that these people can come under the jurisdiction of the provinces and have access near their homes, to the care they deserve.

Very specific conditions and guarantees were written into these contracts. J can assure the hon. member for Vaudreuil that the same conditions will surely be written into the transfer of the hospital in his constituency about which he has the right to question us and which, I can assure him, will be carried out. While details may vary a little from province to province, the broad overriding principles remain the same. There must be assurances for adequate hospital treatment and accommodations for departmental patients.
The hon. member for Vaudreuil quoted a news release on October 21 last which had to do with the transfer of Queen Mary hospital. From that news release I would like to quote two paragraphs:
Queen Mary Veterans Hospital opened in 1945 to provide high level acute care to injured service men and women returning from the war. Throughout its history, the primary mission has been the care of the war-related conditions of disability pensioners who reside in the Montreal area.
Then I come to a very important paragraph.
From its inception, under the guidance of eminent Montreal physicians, and later in association with McGill University and the University of Montreal, the Hospital has enjoyed an enviable continent-wide reputation for its pioneer reconstructive work with the seriously injured.
We have every assurance that this type of care that has been given to our veterans, and which they have coming to them, will continue in the months and the years ahead.

If I might continue, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that you can see from the things that I have talked about that the government takes its moral responsibility for hospital and medical treatment of veterans very seriously. We know that our disability pensioners are getting older and that they need, primarily, facilities for treatment of a chronic care nature. At the same time it is important that they should have available to them the full range of modern medical and hospital care the instant that the need is evident.
We know that we cannot attract the staff to give them this modern, specialized care in existing veterans' hospitals. It is unthinkable that we should allow these hospitals to deteriorate into second class institutions, suitable only for the care of the aged; and inadequate care at that. All of the factors that went into the equations of establishing special hospitals for veterans have changed. Therefore, new equations must be worked out. We feel that the policy of transferring veteran patients into the total community medical care complex with built-in safeguards for the veterans who are our responsibility, and for hospital staff also, is not only the best possible solution to the problem but it gives the veteran patients highly desirable options that they did not have before. Let me elaborate a little bit on that point.

Mr. Speaker, under current programs veterans can choose their physician. They can also choose the hospital where they want to be treated. This means that from now on veterans will no longer have to travel from 50 to 200 miles to go to a hospital and see a doctor with whom they may not be acquainted. They will now be in a position to choose their own physician and receive the necessary care so that they will get everything they need to lead a normal life. They will now have the opportunity, Mr. Speaker, of being hospitalized near the towns where they live. If they do not like the physician they have chosen, they may see another one.

In most cases it is only a short car ride away from the home of the dischargee. Anyone who has ever been in a hospital would agree that these are significant advantages. I am sure that you can see, Mr. Speaker, that the hospital transfer policy is anything but an abrogation of responsibility on the part of the government. Quite the reverse is true. The right of the veterans to the best possible medical and hospital care available is the principle upon which all agreements are negotiated.

Mr. Speaker, before you interrupted me at five o'clock to accommodate private members' hour and the supper hour, I was paying tribute to a number of speakers who had preceded me and who had made a very eloquent case on behalf of the Canadian fisheries, which are now to be restored to their proper place within the organizational structure of government.

I feel it my duty to add to the one and a half to two lines the environment minister devoted to Canadian forestry in his contribution to the debate. After he was finished with the notes which had been prepared for him by his department, he did try to defend the indefensible, namely, the latest government action to phase out a number of very important components of the Canadian Forestry Service. The minister is attempting to pass on to the provinces and to the private sector a number of very important research and development responsibilities.
In his remarks the minister became a little excited. He also attributed certain comments to me, and I think I had better take this opportunity to correct his misconception. For instance, he told the House that he had heard me say, in the House and in other places, that I am in favour of the Kitimat pipeline. Well, I do not know where the minister heard that. Let me say that I am not opposed to the Kitimat pipeline. Obviously the minister knows best what is good for the oil industry and what is good for Kitimat, Prince Rupert, and the area which is the responsibility of the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mrs. Campagnolo). She too is opposed to the pipeline.
I do not know on what grounds these two ministers have made their assessments, because, after all, as the House knows, it was the government which phased out what we consider to have been a very important inquiry, namely, the Thompson inquiry, which was studying that particular project and also the alternatives that are available to us for accommodating our neighbours to the south in getting their oil to midwest refineries. The oil has to get down somehow, and some of the alternatives which the government chose not to consider are much less attractive than the Kitimat pipeline would be. I would advise my friends on the other side of the House to consult with their own constituents, with their mayors, municipalities and chambers of commerce, all of whom have probably paid much more attention to the proposals relating to the Kitimat pipeline and who have, as well, made their own assessment of the immediate, lasting, significant, and positive side effects that such a project would have.
I am getting away from the topic of tonight's debate, Mr. Speaker. I said before the dinner hour that I would want to state the case for the forest industry which remains under the jurisdiction of the Minister of State for the Environment (Mr. Marchand) and which has undergone reorganization in 1973, and is now buried even further after the latest attempt in the basements and in the hindmost thoughts of Ottawa bureaucracy to reorganize it. The debate on fisheries was so eloquent that I thought that to demonstrate the force of the forest industry in our country I should quote some statistics, making some interesting comparisons between the forest industry and the contribution it makes to our economy, and fisheries. Statistics are, of course, always outdated. These were compiled in 1974 and some in 1976, but they are very interesting, to say the least.

Fish products manufacturing-this does not include landing-was $10,100,000 in 1974. Wood products manufacturing, not including logging, which gives you an adequate assessment, was $77,800,000, whereas pulp and paper manufacturing in 1974 was $92 million. When you add that to the primary products you find that fisheries was $291 million, forestry was $1,220,000, manufacturing, fish processing was $225 million, wood manufacturing and processing was $1,708,000, pulp and paper combined was $3,033.7 million. In sales, fish produced in 1974 was $55.4 million, forestry was $530.3 million, ten times the amount for fisheries. Manufacturing, fish processing was $818.5 million, wood manufacturing and pulp and paper combined were roughly $13 million. The value of exports-this is a really interesting statistic-was the following in 1976: fish and fish products were $579.4 million, and all forest products were $6,501.8 million. In corporate income taxes-again these figures are from Statistics Canada-forestry, including logging, was $14.5 million, fishing and trapping was $.4 million, fish processing was $7 million, wood manufacturing was $59.1 million, and pulp and paper was $306.8 million.
To put the picture into real focus one would also have to provide statistics that would show the kind of subsidy and support that has been given to these two industries by the taxpayers. One would see then that the fishing industry has been heavily subsidized throughout the years, whereas the forestry sector receives no subsidy from either the federal or provincial taxpayer.
It is not my intention, of course, to belittle the importance of the crucial component, the fisheries industry, in our total economic picture. However, the fact is that forestry has been the backbone and the mainstay of the economic well-being of this country for a long, long time. Indeed, the $6 billion favourable trade balance owing to forest related industries creates a vivid contrast with the $5 billion which we receive for all the fuel and minerals which we export, and is also in contrast with the figures of $1 billion for agriculture and $.3 billion for fisheries.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) told us today in the House that the governor of the Bank of Canada had certain suggestions to make regarding the minimum requirements to get our economy back into shape, and one of these requirements was that Canada be much more aggressive in seeking new export markets for our primary manufactured goods. Forestry is one sector that is probably best situated and best equipped to increase immediately our exports to foreign countries.
Let me quote a few additional statistics which place the forest sector in our economy in a proper perspective. The forest resource supports 300,000 jobs directly, and up to 700,000 jobs indirectly in secondary manufacturing and in the service industries. The forest products industry in Canada is the leading commodity sector in terms of sales, employment, exports, earnings, and regional dispersion. We speak about fisheries every day in this House, but do we ever hear someone speak about forestry? Certainly the minister responsible for that
