speechtext:
Canadian forests are an important factor in our $3 billion outdoor recreation industry. The federal government receives $1 billion from forestry activities in revenue, while the provincial governments collect roughly $650 million in forest related taxes.
I expect that the House will, some day in the very near future, give recognition to that important sector and, I hope, restore it to its rightful position. I do not assume that that will happen because of the staggering statistics I have just mentioned, but I do believe that the time is foreseeable when our forest industry will face the same kind of crisis which finally prompted the government to take drastic and positive action with regard to fisheries. My friend and colleague, the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain), has quoted some statistics supporting this statement.
With the indulgence of the House, I should like to make the following comments: Canada's share of world export markets for forest products has decreased from 31 per cent to 19 per cent in the last 20 years, while the United States' share has increased from less than 9 per cent to more than 12 per cent. Canada, with 13 per cent of the world's softwood timber resources, produces only 11 per cent of the world's harvest of softwoods, whereas the United States, with 11 per cent of the same resource, harvests 22 per cent of the world's total. The general productivity in the wood industry in Canada is 15 per cent less than that in the United States. Canada, with a forest industry which provides direct and indirect employment for nearly one million people and contributes almost one fifth of the nation's exports, finds itself with serious problems emerging with regard to economic supplies of timber. Federally funded research and development at forest products laboratories is approximately $14 million in the United States, compared with $7 million in Canada. After the latest cutbacks and slashes which the minister undertook on behalf of the government, the contrast will be more dramatic. Referring to the United States, the following comments appear in an Environment Canada news release:
State expenditure on forest products research provides large scale facilities in Oregon, California, Michigan and Mississippi, but no provincial counterparts exist in Canada-
University expenditure on forest products research is about $6 million in the United States, but only $200,000 in Canada-
A single United States company, Weyerhaeuser, spends almost twice as much annually on research and development as the entire Canadian forestry service- The man-years available to the Canadian forestry service have decreased by 50 per cent over the last decade, during which significant manpower growth has occurred in nearly every other facet of the federal public service-
The lumber and solid wood products industry in Canada spends .08 per cent of sales on R and D compared with .84 per cent for all other industries. The wood processing industry thereby ranks last in R and D expenditures among the 20 leading industrial sectors in Canada.

The budget of the Canadian forestry service will be slashed a further $5.3 million-15 per cent-in 1979.
There are pages and pages of similar statistics and horror stories, yet the minister attempts to defend what he has done recently.
As we all know, the government is capable only of reacting to crises. The forest industry of this country is the mainstay of our industrial capacity, and indeed it will face a very serious crisis in short order. There is not yet a crisis in the forest industry. But the Minister of Finance, who is present in the House tonight, has managed to bring about a decline in our dollar. This has provided a cushion and some breathing space for the industry. However, in the meantime we continue the old art of hewing wood and drawing water. Our efforts to generate new growth and to reforest or replant logged-off areas are hopelessly inadequate in every Canadian province.
There are literally millions of acres of prime forest land which have not been replanted. There is no leadership or direction from any source, either provincial or federal, to encourage provincial or federal agencies or the industry itself to undertake the task of replanting and renewing our forests.
At the present time there are serious shortages of supplies. Companies in timber producing provinces are now discovering that much of the timber allocated to them by the provincial governments cannot be harvested with conventional methods, because the timber is located in remote areas and present techniques are not adequate enough to move into these areas. Of course the economic constraints facing these companies do not allow them to expand their operations in these areas.
We are discovering that estimates of wood inventory are badly distorted, and that our timber supply position is in a most precarious state. This is one area in which the industry and the provinces have repeatedly asked the federal government for assistance to establish an inventory throughout the country. This would provide us with a much better assessment of our timber supply position in the foreseeable future.
In his speech last night the minister was quite sensitive. He responded to criticism from this side of the House respecting the latest reform which was necessary as a result of the government's action to cut programs. The minister attempted to defend phasing out the Forest Management Institute in Ottawa and moving it to Petawawa. Also he attempted to defend the move of the fire institute to Petawawa. Of course it increased the manpower at that particular station, but it decreased the services and programs which were carried on before. The minister is inclined to lay blame for all difficulties in the forest sector on the shoulders of industry and the provinces.
The concept of privatization has been bandied around in the House. The minister decided that the forest products laboratories should be privatized. The industry relies heavily upon the laboratories to arrive at new techniques, produce new products, and to help it become as efficient as its counterpart in the United States. The federal government made the decision to phase out these facilities in Vancouver and Ottawa. It has requested that private industry assume the responsibility of
January 25, 1979

carrying on these efforts. I have nothing to say against such a concept. Private industry always has been very co-operative when it came to protecting, preserving, and enhancing harvesting opportunities and the conversion of a natural resource. In this particular case, I speak as a person who has some experience in the industry.
I would be reluctant to have larger corporations providing manpower to travel around the country, passing the hat in order to pick up the required $3.2 million to sustain the efforts of forest laboratories. For example, I would be reluctant if MacMillan-Bloedel or some other forest giant in the country were put in charge of providing all the research required by industry. Private industry of that corporate quality always has had its own research facilities and has accepted the responsibility of doing the required research to pursue its own selfish interests. It is not necessarily so that such research is geared to the legitimate and selfish interests of smaller wood converting companies, truck loggers, people who harvest trees, and the small sawmills which are not as integrated as the forest giants. As a result of the travels of the minister's cronies, I presume large companies will phase out their own research facilities and pay the money which becomes available as a result of their travels into a fund, and under their direction, the federal government will continue research. Whether that will be entirely in the interests of industry and resources is very questionable, as far as I am concerned.
For the benefit of the House I should like to give a short assessment of why the Government of Canada and the governments of the provinces are directly responsible to carry on the research which was carried out by the forest laboratories in Vancouver and Ottawa, as well as the other research institutions through the country. After all, it is the federal government which benefits most from forest activity. As I have stated, the federal government pockt.s roughly $1 billion annually in taxes from forest related industries. The provinces collect an additional $650 million from royalty and stumpage assessments from the industry. The industry throughout this country has been taxed, stumpaged and regulated to death.
Let me give you a profile of what happens to the forest industry in British Columbia, for instance, where the provincial government walks into a plant, makes an assessment of its efficiency and capacity, and then tells the manager and owners that they should be able to produce a thousand board feet of lumber at a certain price. Let us take a figure out of the air, and it probably will not be far out. Let us say you can produce a thousand board feet of lumber at a cost of $150. The provincial forest service then turns around and says that a weekly publication which gives the world price for a thousand board feet of lumber shows the weekly price as $200. It is then apparent that there is a spread of $50 with which the company has to work.
In an attempt to cream off much of this revenue, and to keep the federal tax collector within certain limits, the province simply says that since it costs $150 to produce that
Government Organization
commodity it will allow the operator a 15 per cent margin and the rest will be royalty or stumpage. The plant operates on a 15 per cent margin which, of course, is taxable by a federal agency which imposes a levy or a log tax, which is unique also to British Columbia. From this margin the company has to pay all the other licensing fees, satisfy pollution control and, of course, pay a number of other bookkeeping costs which are required monthly by both the federal and provincial governments. There is no end to the influence these silent partners in Ottawa and in the provinces assert on the industry.
As we debate the concept of privatization of research and development activities we should put the problem in its proper perspective. Governments get the lion's share of profits from forest related activities and, of course, it has to be a government of some sort, provincial or federal, that should return some of the revenues to that sector. I find little comfort in the fact that a few corporate managers are representatives and also, I assume, supporters of the Liberal cause, who make the offer to the minister to travel around the country passing the hat to collect the few dollars which will be necessary in the foreseeable future to sustain the efforts of research laboratories.
I would like you to consider, sir, how you would feel, having worked for the government or for a company for 15 or more years, giving the best years of your life, to be told without proper notice that your job has been phased out, but someone has been travelling around the country to take up a collection to see if you can be kept on. If that is the way this government treats its public servants I sincerely hope the public servants and others throughout this country will have a chance soon to reciprocate by treating this government in the same way.
I have never been one to stand in this House to criticize without offering, or at least making some suggestions that could help the situation we are debating. For instance, sir, I fully believe it should be the onus of industry to pay for the research and development that needs to be done to upgrade this important industry, making it more efficient and making it more competitive with our trading partners offshore.
There is a simple solution, one that has been suggested not just by myself. I have discussed it with the minister personally, who seemed at the time to be in agreement. It is a suggestion that has been made by both the industry and the provinces, as well as by professionals. It is simply to enter into an agreement with the provinces to raise, as part of their royalty or stumpage assessment, a certain sum of money. A levy of 50 cents per thousand board feet, something that would not hurt anybody, would generate $6 million annually in British Columbia alone. I have not had time to work out what that would generate throughout the country. Clearly when one considers that companies pay up to $35 per thousand board feet of lumber in stumpage, another 50 cents would not hurt. It certainly would not hurt the provinces either if we took that 50 cents from the revenue they are already getting from the industry. In this way the taxpayer would not carry this burden, and the industry, having paid for the research and for the development of new species, and whatever other things the institutes were into,

1 should like to make the point that if the minister feels he would not have the support of the provincial governments or the industry, he just has not been talking to them lately. Indeed, the Forest Management Institute, an arm of the federal government, commissioned a report which is today referred to and read with almost biblical reverence throughout the country. F.L.C. Reed Associates Ltd. published a report last year which was commissioned by the Forest Management Institute. That report has been made available to the minister. The Reed group dealt with all these statistics I have put on the record today, and in clear terms outlined the crucial importance of the industry, first of all, and the crisis situation in which the industry Finds itself today. Let me just quote a short paragraph in relation to some of the recommendations included in the report, as follows:
A single agency should act as spokesman on forest policy and as co-ordinator of related programs. This would help to restore forestry to its deserved status. A strengthened Canadian forestry service is the logical agency for this function. Its duties should include allocation of federal money to forestry projects on a continuing basis and subsequent monitoring of progress.
I would like to put on record another short quotation which comes directly from the minister's office. I do not recall this report being tabled in the House. It is the third report which was made by the Canadian Forestry Advisory Council, to the Minister of the Environment and it is dated September, 1975. Like the recommendations that have been made on behalf of the fishing industry, this report says under the heading "Recommendations and National Forest Policy":
The need for a national forest policy statement is all the more urgent because most provinces are now giving priority to provincial forest policy development. Divided jurisdictions will, however, make the formulation of a meaningful

national policy difficult. Once agreement is reached on objectives, mutually compatible federal, provincial and industrial guidelines must be developed to give co-ordinated direction to industry and management...
In order to redress the status of forestry at the national level, and to give leadership in developing a national forest policy, it is strongly recommended that a minister of state for forestry be appointed whose powers, duties and functions with respect to forestry legislation, and whose mandate to assist the Minister of Environment in forestry affairs, should be comparable to those of the minister of state for fisheries.
These recommendations by qualified bodies of researchers and consultants have been ignored. They will go on being ignored until such time as this most important industry finds itself in the same kind of crisis the Fishing industry has been in for some time, and as I have said, that crisis is within the foreseeable future.
We are losing our competitive position in world markets. The only thing which keeps the industry floating at this point is the devalued Canadian dollar. We in this House must appreciate the valuable contribution this industry has made to our history and our way of life. Forestry is not simply an economic component of our way of life. It has much to do with our social behaviour as well.
The forests in our country are a vital part of our eco-system. Forests generate our water, clean air, and a healthy and prosperous Canadian life. Let us not continue to disobey the requirements and rules regarding our responsibilities to our forests.

1 will not speak long, Mr. Speaker, on this bill as it is a housekeeping bill. The proposal to create a department of fisheries and oceans is one which I think is vital to the fishing industry. The change is a recognition of the importance to the present and the future well-being of the fishing industry, which in the last few years has grown beyond the expectations of the 1960s into a billion dollar industry. It gives the minister of fisheries a clear mandate to provide the leadership and direction to oversee the federal government's activities within the industry, to develop policies relating to fisheries activities, and to consult with all segments of the Fishing industry.
This bill also proposes to create a separate department for the environment, which shows the concern of this government and the recognition by it that both these departments will play an increased role in Canadian life in the future.
I am also pleased with Part II of this bill which deals with the fisheries and oceans research advisory council. In reading over this part, the amendment will provide for an expanded council. Although the section states who will be eligible to sit on the council, I suggest that the section be made clearer and state that there be an even distribution of fishermen from all parts of the country represented on it. I am sure that their contribution will be invaluable.
This bill also allows me to speak about fishing on the east coast, particularly as it relates to southwestern Nova Scotia. The Fishermen on the east coast have been fortunate to have this present minister of fisheries. He has been a full-time minister and has fulFilled a promise which was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the constituency of South
January 25, 1979

Western Nova in June, 1974. The minister has urged the fishermen to organize in order to best relate their needs to both the provincial and federal departments. He has decentralized the federal department so as to better reach those directly concerned with the fishery.
A good example of the decentralization is the Yarmouth federal fisheries building. In the last two years we have had an area manager who deals with matters at the local level. This building provides all the facilities fishermen need with regard to their work. I would also like to take this opportunity to express my good wishes to the retiring area manager for Yarmouth, Mr. Glen Smith, who has worked in the fishery department for many years. His excellent knowledge in that area will be missed by all. I welcome the new area manager and wish him luck in a very difficult area.
For the last three years the fishing industry has benefited from the 200-mile limit, and the returns can be seen throughout Nova Scotia and other areas of the Atlantic. A dramatic increase in the landed value of the fish catch was recorded in the first nine months of 1978. The catch for the Atlantic region had a landed value increase of 49 per cent over the record increase of 1977. The size of the catch rose 21 per cent. The remarkable increases demonstrate the success of federal fishery policy. The minister has turned a herring fishery, which previously concentrated on fish meal, into a viable food industry. Last summer it had an estimated landed value of $17.6 million compared with a value of $12.4 million in 1977, $6.5 million in 1976, and $5.8 million in 1975, despite the fact that last summer was a bad year because fewer herring were landed in the Bay of Fundy area. The minister worked with the fishermen, the industry and the provincial governments to achieve this outstanding success with little cost to the Canadian taxpayer.
In the past three years companies in the fishing industry in South Western Nova have expanded. This is made quite clear from the amount of assistance which has been given to fish companies. I am informed that $1.5 million was awarded as incentive grants to fish companies through the Department of Regional Economic Expansion between 1974 and 1978. This minister has made it his policy, which I hope he will incorporate into the new department, to look first at the fish available and how best to provide for everyone, never forgetting the backbone of the industry-the fishermen, including the smaller fishermen who have been forgotten by many in the industry in the past. If the fishermen are working to full productivity, it follows that the plants are also working.
We hear about the need for freezer trawlers. I for one would say to the minister, "go slowly." In fact, I wonder if we need them at all. We are just now becoming efficient with the existing fleet. We already have shortages in our traditional fisheries. Perhaps we should look at some of the existing fishing boats and determine whether or not they can be used to catch these underutilized species rather than investing in the high cost of freezer trawlers.
Government Organization
I can understand why the foreigners needed freezer trawlers. They came from far away. But do we need them when we are so close to the fishing grounds and can return quickly to shore with our catches? I agree with the minister when he says that we have to improve the existing fishing capabilities before turning to freezer trawlers, which may be very detrimental to the fishery if not properly investigated. After all, it was the same companies which are asking for these freezer trawler boats now which felt the foreign fleets were depleting their fleet capabilities four years ago.
A freezer trawler, in order to pay for itself, is going to need a large catch. Let us ask these questions: whose fish will they catch? Who will be allocated the permits for the freezer trawlers? Will the fishermen themselves be able to go into this, or will it be the companies? Will the province take part in this and allocate the fish from these freezer trawlers to the various plants located all over the Atlantic provinces? Do we need them at all? All these questions at a time when we have just begun to reap the returns of the 200-mile limit, have to be answered before any Canadian freezer trawlers can be allowed to rape our fishery.
Let me now turn to small craft harbours. In South Western Nova, for example, where harbours have been long neglected, we have had major multi-million dollar harbours built since July, 1974, at West Head, Yarmouth, and Meteghan. In addition, there has been major wharf construction or reconstruction at Argyle, Pinkney Point, Pembroke, Cape St. Mary, Tiverton and Freeport, not to mention the work that has been carried out at other harbours such as Smithville, Southside, Woods Harbour, Saulnierville, Sandy Cove East and Sand-ford. This is to mention but a few areas where work has been carried out. This year, again, I am anticipating major undertakings. I look to Wedgepoint getting under way with a $2 million wharf facility in the very near future, and a decision for a deep water harbour on Digby Neck. Dredging and reconstruction are needed on the south wharf at Dennis Point, work at Westport, Short Beach, Port Maitland and a floating breakwater at Cape Forchu are a few of the needed repairs in this area.
Another innovative area that this Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) can take praise for is the assistance given by the small craft harbours branch to the Canada Works Program. Funds under Canada Works Program and capital expenditures from small craft harbours have provided slipways, haulouts, additions to wharves and general upkeep, as well as providing an input from the fishermen for the use of these funds from the Canada Works Program.
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to discuss the matter of jurisdiction. There seems to be a lot of discussion on this word lately and I will approach this last topic as it relates to two areas of great concern in my area as a representative from the east coast. One is the federal jurisdiction in fisheries, on which I will be brief and say that in terms of quotas, surveillance, research, quality, inspection and markets-and the latter three as far as they relate to international markets-

January 25, 1979
Government Organization
it would appear to me that the federal government must be the supreme power over these areas. We cannot control the areas where fish gather or travel-I can see fish wars developing between eastern provinces as to how and when they can fish. We have seen what happened with the foreigners who were fishing off our shores prior to the 200-mile limit and we have seen what happened between Canada and the United States on George's Bank, but we should control at a federal level how the industry is going to approach all of these areas within our 200-mile limit.
In my opinion, when a final decision on a fishery matter has to be made, and someone has to make it, that decision should rest with the federal department of fisheries since they can take all provinces into consideration.
The second point I wish to make with regard to jurisdiction is on the Canada-U.S. bilateral negotiations. I would like to discuss George's Bank which, as all members are fully aware, is of great concern to the southern part of Nova Scotia. Perhaps more than any other area of Canada, the people in that area realize how important this area is, not only because of its good fishing grounds but because traditionally the fishermen of Southwestern Nova Scotia have always gone to Georges Bank to fish. I am glad to see that the negotiators have recommended that the boundary dispute be sent to a third party. All of us are no doubt anxious to see what the negotiations will have accomplished in the allocation of the various fisheries which exist on George's Bank.
Different provinces have sent observers from government and from industry to the negotiations, and these people were asked to brief the negotiators with their views. With this in mind, I cannot help but feel that this has been truly one area where the industry, the provinces, and the federal government, have discussed what the future fishing arrangements and negotiations should be as they relate to George's Bank, and I look forward to hearing the proposals which the negotiators are putting forth to their respective governments.
One thing that the minister cannot be criticized for is the consultation that he has had with the fishermen and the industry. I do not recall any other minister responsible for the fishery, or any other person responsible for the fishery, having as many meetings with industry. He has told the fishermen to organize, and they have. He has organized the herring fishery. Seiners have been able to talk to him, as have weir fishermen and gillnetters. This week a representative of the gillnetters of South Western Nova talked to the minister in Ottawa.
The hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) said there has been no consultation in the lobster fishery, but I remember that at the end of 1974 a lobster task force held meetings in Digby, Meteghan, Yarmouth and Barrington, to mention a few of the areas across Nova Scotia that happen to be in my constituency. The results were different categories and a buyback arrangement. There must be built into that buy-back an opportunity for the young fishermen to gain entry into the fishery.
We have had the closing of Brown's Bank, which was sorely needed to save the inshore lobster fishery. Personally I feel

that Brown's Bank should be closed to all boats over 65 feet. The licensing arrangements are being examined in consultation with the fishermen and the officials. I hope to see a policy regarding boats of 45 feet and under which will allow all fishermen access to all the fishery.
In conclusion let me say, Mr. Speaker, that over the past four and one half years there have been consultations between the provincial and federal governments, between fishermen, industry and governments. The credit for this has to rest with the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. He has been aware of the problems and, in my opinion, Canadians on both coasts and in the mid-west have a full time minister of fisheries.

Mr. Speaker, I want for a few moments to refer to other clauses of this bill that have not received any or just brief attention in the debate to this point as far as I know. I refer specifically to Part VI with respect to the Medical Research Council, Part VII with respect to the National Research Council, Part VIII, the National Sciences and Engineering Research Council, and Part IX, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council.
Let me indicate at the outset that these parts are very similar to a bill that we debated during the latter part of 1976. At that time I spoke about some aspects of the legislation which dealt with the reorientation of the scientific organization. I have no intention of reviewing the content of my speech at that time, but I think two or three points are pertinent. I did raise the most important question not only as to the entire science policy in Canada but specifically the future of the Ministry of State for Science and Technology. We have seen what has happened to that particular ministry with the passage of time. It has been downplayed. Indeed its significance as a major ministry in this government has deteriorated with the passage of time.
As a matter of fact I indicated that I was quite pleased with the formation of the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council. I can recall vividly in the Speech from the Throne in 1974 there was a great deal of interest given to the Ministry of State for Science and Techonology. At that time there was thought given to forming a natural science research council as no consideration at all had been given to the importance of engineering research. That I thought was a positive move. But, most important, at that time I raised the basic issue of financial commitment to research. It is in this
January 25, 1979

sense that I wanted to speak for a few moments tonight specifically with respect to the medical research council.
Many of us on this side of the house have pursued this issue with a great deal of vigour, certainly I have since 1972 when I came to the House of Commons. I must say that despite the pronouncements of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) in the early part of December, 1978, I am not convinced that this government understands the importance of medical research in Canada, the role it has played in the past, the role it could play now, and the role it could play in the future. I am amazed because as I have dealt with people in the past and as I have travelled across Canada I have found that virtually every family has had a member or perhaps even a friend afflicted with some illness or some type of disease. I am absolutely certain in my mind that individuals are concerned about these problems and are most interested in a government or any group that would demonstrate an interest in medical research and support it in an appropriate manner.
If one looks at newspapers over a period of time, I believe this is demonstrated by their editorials. For example, I can remember in the early 1940 there were many editorials at that time concerned about the side effects of lead poisoning. There were a number of children in Canada who had problems with lead poisoning and people were asking for increased research with respect to lead poisoning.
I have seen articles on the problems of aging and the importance of research in this area. There are articles on megavitamins and the significance they may have with respect to the health of individuals in our society.
I recall in the early 1970s there was a good deal of discussion as to how much research was being done in Canada with respect to matters such as acupuncture and what effect it might have in terms of being an anesthetic tool or in treating diseases, particularly those of a painful nature. Also in the early 1970s we can recall the problems associated with mercury pollution when that problem arrived on the scene. Editorials were asking why there was no additional research for mercury poisoning. And indeed when we had the opposition day in this House of Commons with respect to mercury poisoning that was one of the elements of the debate which was raised at that time.
I can recall during the days of the Le Dain Commission people across the country were asking why we did not have more research concerning marijuana and other hard drugs. One could go on and on. For example, cigarette smoking and cancer can be mentioned. As I have mentioned, there is an editorial interest and there is an interest in Canada in terms of this most important aspect of medical research. But two or three other things come to mind. I am sure in addition to the items I have listed there are many other targets and areas of research that are important. One thing that people and the government should recognize is the fact that researchers cannot be trained overnight. It is a prolonged process. To have outstanding researchers it takes years of practice. This must be built up over a period of time with a great deal of patience and a great deal of cost.
Government Organization
Another aspect that must be remembered, as I have indicated, is that we need a broad front. In other words our targets tend to change from day to day, from week to week, and from month to month. What is perceived to be important in terms of a research topic today may not seem to be as relevant tomorrow. Something more important may appear on the scene tomo.row. That implies that if we are to provide that type of service, and if we are to provide the basic scientific and the basic biomedical research necessary, then we must have a broad front for basic medical research in Canada.
I will attempt to define and enlarge on this a little later. We must recognize, and I have pointed this out before-perhaps I can try to explain it in a little more detail this evening-that we cannot divorce basic medical research from education and from the delivery of health care across Canada. Indeed I suppose one could include preventive type medicine itself. They are interrelated, sir. If one of the links is weakened in the chain, I can assure hon. members that the quality of health care will disappear.
I have heard individuals and senior government officials on the other side from time to time indicate that it is much cheaper to import a health science. I found that remarkably strange and I am not sure that I follow the logic of that. Think about it for a moment. We are now talking about a very high technology of basic research and assume we have the hypothetical situation that we do not have the capability in Canada because we are going to import it.
I ask hon. members do you know who the knowledgeable people are who can assess that type of basic research that is done elsewhere in the international community? Where is the type of environment, the symposia or the type of consultative process that one would have in Canada that can really handle that in a proper fashion? Who, sir, would have the knowledge to interpret such fundamental basic research that could then be applied appropriately and even determine if it was applicable in a very human and real sense in terms of the medical problems in Canada?
Another matter that bothers me considerably is hearing officials from time to time, within government and elsewhere, who say that people are not prepared to finance medical research across Canada. Frankly I do not accept that statement, for a number of reasons. I find it amazing, because as I recall there are funds set up across Canada totalling around $600 million which contribute roughly $20 million to medical research of one sort or another each year. That is a substantial amount of money that has been donated by private individuals for the most important area of basic research.
It does not matter whether one looks at the Heart Fund or Muscular Dystrophy or the March of Dimes-I could go on and on listing these types of programs. It is my perception that people are very generous in their support of this type of program which is for basic research. Within the last two or three years a great proportion of the money devoted to cancer research, I believe roughly in the neighbourhood of $5 million or $6 million this past year, came from the private sector, not from the federal government.

January 25, 1979
Government Organization
As I indicated at the outset, there seems to be an uncertainty in the mind of the government as to the importance of biomedical research. I want to spend a few moments tonight, because I do not believe this has been done in the past to any great extent, trying to demonstrate to this government the importance of biomedical or basic research in Canada. I want to do that by reviewing some of the biomedical research that has led to the improvement of health care of individuals across Canada.
Before I give specific areas of research, let me indicate that in the whole area of biomedical research, and I think this is most important, that an individual working on project X may well end up with results that are not relative necessarily to that project. But they may have great relevance to another area that is being assessed, analysed or studied in another part of the country. Let us look at some of the biomedical research that has contributed to the health of not only Canadians but people in the international context.
First, polio. I am sure we have all heard of all the various vaccines and so forth. Let me remind hon. members that the original breakthrough in the polio vaccine originated from another project in which polio vaccine was not the anticipated end result. Think about it for a moment. If we had not had that breakthrough and had not had the polio vaccine, we would be living with the mentalities of the thirties and forties, with iron lungs and all of this massive, expensive technology which has been cured by the introduction and discovery of a simple vaccine.
We know, for example, that Enders basic research paved the way for Salk's polio vaccine, which, incidentally, was somewhat different from the original polio vaccine when it was introduced by Sabin. It has been estimated that since 1955 there have been accumulated about 50,000 Canadians whose lives were spared by these vaccines which were developed for polio. Economists have estimated that is an annual saving of approximately $200 million per year in Canada. We must think also about the human suffering that has been eliminated by the introduction of such a vaccine.
Waksman's discovery in 1955 of streptomycin at Rutger's University in the United States was a milestone in the treatment of tuberculosis. A number of years ago, before the introduction of appropriate therapy, individuals with that disease were institutionalized for six months or a year. Now, with appropriate therapy, it is not inconceivable that they are returned home within a two or three week period on adequate therapy. Think of the savings in costs and the relief of human suffering in terms of that discovery.
Basic research in immunology was carried out in Liverpool with respect to mental retardation. It was most significant in terms of hemalytic problems that occurred in newborn children. Of course we see this with Rh negative mothers. That situation has virtually been eliminated by that very basic biomedical research.
[Mr. Holmes.)
Hepatitis, a very, very common problem and a very expensive one in the past, was eliminated by the discovery, and I may say accidentally, by Blumberg in Australia of an antiprotein substance that was very effective in assisting in recognizing this disease, saving incalculable millions of dollars a year and the associated human suffering.
I could go on-Dausset in France, Payne in the United States who improved the tissue matching for kidney transplants. We now see these patients surviving for a much longer period of time. It has been estimated there is a saving of at least $10 million to $20 million a year with this one basic research discovery.
I could turn to Dr. Judith Pool of Stanford and her basic, almost accidental, discovery of how to prepare simply large amounts of anti-hemophilic protein for the treatment of hemophilics, a most important problem. I recall in the past that without adequate treatment, hemophiliacs had a very prolonged stay in hospital. We had very limited tools in our possession. We talked of hospital stays that could cost $10,000 or $20,000 a year for a family before the days of hospitalization insurance. That has virtually been eliminated with that type of discovery.
Another area is the anti-psychotic drugs that were discovered. These were primarily produced in France in the fifties. I am not exaggerating when I say, and 1 think the facts will prove it, probably 100,000 people a year are kept out of our hospitals and mental institutions. They are kept at home for a far more prolonged period because of the discovery and introduction of this type of drug. I am sure hon. members can appreciate the cost involved without that type of biomedical research.
Let us look in the Canadian context. Many are familiar with all individuals here-Banting and Best for the discovery of insulin. Need I say any more? We all know what that has saved in terms of dollars to individuals in Canada. There is also the possibility of the prospect of being able to treat that disease in a far more responsible way than we could years ago.
There is also the test for determining a person's sex by Dr. Barr, a former professor of mine at the University of Western Ontario. If I may say, sir, I am sure that name rings a bell with you. It is a very international name, he is a great Canadian, well known in international circles.
Think of what Dr. Gold of Montreal has done in terms of basic research on cancer. There is the work of Dr. Barbeau and his colleagues on L-DOPA, a most impressive drug in the treatment of Parkinson's disease. Two or three years ago in this House we were talking about mercury pollution and discussing Dr. Barbeau's name. He is internationally known as a neurologist and neurosurgeon who is working on the Minimata disease with the Cree Indians in northern Quebec.
I am trying to make a point that has not been recognized by this government as to the importance of basic medical research. Let me go on a little further. I think this is most significant. I really want the government to get the message as to the importance of basic medical research in this country.
January 25, 1979

I remember when Dr. Charles Scriver appeared before the standing committee, at our insistence. We had been asking, and continue to ask this government to take positive action with regard to medical research in Canada. In one of his appendices he had what I considered to be very interesting information which may help elucidate the importance of this problem of research. In it he had a consensus on advances in medicine. He asked 40 physician consultants and 40 to 50 specialists in cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases, and I am now talking about problems relating to the heart and lungs, to select the top ten major advances in that area over the past 30 years. This is the consensus.
Rated number one was cardiac surgery. What does he mean by cardiac surgery? He is referring to open heart surgery or repair of valves. The second was vascular surgery. That, of course, refers to the repair or bypass of various major vessels in the body such as the aorta or ileac vessels.
The third was drug treatment for hypertension or high blood pressure. The fourth was medical treatment of coronary heart disease. The fifth was treatment of cardiac arrest and irregularity of heartbeat.
The sixth was the development of oral diuretics. Let me explain this for hon. members who may not know. A diuretic is used very frequently in the treatment of those individuals who have accumulation, and in this particular instance accumulation of fluid in the chest. Of course, diuretics work on the kidneys in such a way that they excrete an extra amount of fluid.
The seventh was for intensive care units. This was for post-operative patients, coronary patients, respiratory patients, and newborn patients. Let me remind the House again that I am just talking about illnesses related to cardio-pulmonary problems. The eighth was the development of chemotherapy and antibiotics. This is not uncommon, and we are now talking about individuals with rheumatic heart disease, those who develop problems like endocarditis. Included with this were drugs such as I indicated somewhat earlier, streptomycin for tuberculosis, various antipneumonia drugs, various antibiotics, and of course drugs related to some of the venereal diseases which not infrequently could affect the major vessels of the chest.
The ninth was new diagnostic methods, and the tenth was polio vaccine. This may sound strange, but we must remember that there was a marked correlation between respiratory paralysis and polio vaccine in those days.
The government has never recognized the importance of the time frame or the amount of time that is necessary for these advances. As I indicated earlier, in biomedical research you cannot have shooting targets. You must have personnel in a broad area who are working over a period of time. Advances are slow in many instances. There must be accumulation of material and basic medical research in various areas over a period of time. Let me give an example. Dr. Scriver did this very adequately when he was looking at just one example of
Government Organization
open heart surgery. Open heart surgery was first performed in 1954 by Dr. Gibbon. The basic research for that really commenced in 1846. I cannot give all the elements of that research; time will not permit. In 1846 there was the development of general anaesthesia. Anaesthesia was obviously necessary for surgery of any kind at that time. Then we had the development of x-ray. X-ray is not simple. It involves the science of physics and other components.
Then we had to develop basic research regarding cardiac catheterization. We had to have all that technology, plus we had to develop the technology for cardio-pulmonary bypass, and then we had to have all the basic fundamental biochemical and physiological knowledge of oxygen and carbon dioxide, their uptake at the heart and lungs and their passage through the alveolar passages. There was a necessity for developing curare-like anaesthesia. That was developed in Canada, but the point I am trying to make is that to develop to that stage where Dr. Gibbon could do open heart surgery in 1954, we had to go through an entire list of many medical research steps. There had to be accumulation of medical research through projects over a period of years.

Centuries, as my colleague says. This accumulation took place between 1846 and 1954. This is a concept which I really do not believe the government understands. I apologize for taking the time, but I think getting this concept across to the government is absolutely essential. Since I came here in 1972 1 have been convinced that the government really does not grasp the significance of biomedical research.
I want to quote parts of an article which describes the problem very simply. This article refers to a speech which was given by Dr. Lewis Thomas, President of the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Centre in New York.
Imagine this scenario: it takes place in a densely populated city in the northeast. Suppose you had to look after the majority of your patients on open wards, designed, say, for 26 patients each. Now suppose that these wards were kept entirely full, mostly by patients unable to pay anything at all for their care, throughout all 12 months of the year. Imagine that it is now late November, and the wards are not only full but you have had to arrange two rows of cots down the centre of each ward; you now have 40 patients in each 26-bed ward; and you know that within the next few weeks the cots will have to be extended out into the corridor, right up to, and perhaps even occluding, the elevator doors. This is the way things will be until next April, when it will slack off a bit and you can go back to a light service, with maybe only 30 patients on each 26-bed ward.
Now imagine that this arrangement is only the beginning of the demand for service. You need another entire hospital building, built somewhere adjoining the general hospital if you are lucky (for you can then consolidate a few costly service functions) or built in another part of town if you are unlucky. Into this hospital you will have to crowd, during the winter months, about twice the number of patients it is designed to contain. Most of these patients will be young children, and you will have to invent ways to isolate them from each other, and from everyone else.
Now imagine, if you can, that something like half of the patients in this huge nightmare of an institution are at risk of dying because of the severity of their diseases. Not that this number will actually die-indeed, many of them will survive and go home, but they will be deathly ill for weeks before they recover, and you will have to provide medical and nursing care around the clock to bring this off. Moreover, you will have to do this without much in the way of medicine, which means that you must be immensely skilled in the organization of general,

Government Organization
non-specific, supportive measures in order to bring the majority of your patients through.
What I have been describing is, of course, the Boston City Hospital of 35 years ago; but it could be Bellevue, or Cook County, or Brady, or Charity-
It could have been in Alberta, Montreal or Toronto.
-or any large general hospital of that period, and for a great many so-called public hospitals, run by counties or municipalities, the situation was a great deal worse.
Everyone recognized that it was intolerable, and there was no lack of organized public protest and no end to the recommendations by public bodies that something be done to change it. It was an open scandal. The hospitals were crowded beyond the point of inhumanity; there were never enough doctors and nurses to meet the need; too many patients were dying; something had to be done to put a stop to it.
Okay, we fixed it. It took a while, but we accomplished the revolution, and institutions like the crowded Boston City Hospital of 1937 have vanished. The chief problem confronting the city hospitals today is that they are so uncrowded that they can no longer justify anything like their costs of operating. The contagious disease units have been closed down. The tuberculosis hospitals are out of business. It is a different world.
How did we do all this? Some people, most of whom are too young to have lived through the old ways of hospital care, assume that it happened as a result of a social revolution that is still in progress, and that we eliminated the intolerable crowding of city hospitals by changing the economics of health care. The reason we no longer have all those cots down the center of all those open wards is that most of the patients are insured, on way or another, and since they can pay for their care they have gone off to other, more human and habitable, institutions. According to this view, we solved our problem, or anyway that part of the problem, by money.
If this were true, it would obviously carry enormous implications for the future. Having made a quantum improvement in the quality of hospital care between 1937 and today, we could look forward to equivalent improvements in the future, subject only to our ingenuity in finding sufficient funds and seeing to it that they are distributed with something more like equity.
He goes on to say later what really happened at that time. This is what is most important. I hope you will get the graphic picture of the situation which existed at that time. What happened sir, as he goes on to say, is the following:
What happened was that we got rid of lobar pneumonia. This was the main event, surrounded by several others of somewhat less importance. We also got rid of meningococcal meningitis and scarlet fever; the great urban outbreaks of diphtheria finally came under control;
That was the reason that the situation improved, and that is the message I am trying to get across. As a matter of fact, he goes on to say something more, and I think it is important. I want to quote one final paragraph from his paper. He says:
If I were a policymaker, interested in saving money for health care over the long haul, I would regard it as an act of prudence to give a high priority to a lot more basic research in the biological sciences.
That is the message I am trying to get across to this government this evening. That is why I have taken the time to demonstrate so many areas in which advances have been made which not only have been of assistance to individuals in a very human sense but also advances that have been of assistance in the economic sense. I say to the government that there is no question that the biological sciences should be given a high priority for some of the reasons I have outlined.
For a moment or two now I want to review a little of what transpired on the Canadian scene. I think those who are in the House know that during the post war era, particularly during

the 1950s and 1960s, there was a sense of euphoria in the research community. We saw that in the various faculties across the country. Medical schools were expanding, new staff was being hired, faculty posts were being developed, research projects were increasing at a rapid rate. I think that was part of the environmental attitude that existed in Canada at that time. All that has disappeared in the early 1970s.
Perhaps I should add one word here about something that has been poorly understood. We should recognize that scientists who are recruited to this most important area are not there for the financial reward. Those from the medical profession who are interested in that type of financial reward do not go into research. Financial rewards can be found in other areas. When we talk about moneys that are obtained by the important scientists in Canada who do major work, we must recognize that this is not money for their pockets but money for the various programs they are establishing. It is money for the support of their programs and for the technologists and equipment they need. As we all know, they are usually funded in the various chairs, or whatever position they hold in the universities.
As I indicated, in the early 1970s, and certainly since I came to the House of Commons in 1972, we have seen a slow but steady erosion in medical research in Canada. There is no question about that. There is no doubt that the abilities and skills of our investigators were there, but I want to assure you that despite the high quality of the research that existed, which would match any international standards, there has been a slow erosion in the research done in the Canadian scene. Although I indicated previously that the large portion of the funding for medical research comes from the public sector, we must recognize the major funding has come from the Medical Research Council.
If we look over the past nine years, it may appear to us that there has been a significant increase from about $34 million in 1970 to the present budget, which was initially estimated at about $60 million. I do not wish to get into a lot of statistics at this time, but let me point out that there has been a decrease in constant dollars with respect to medical research in Canada. We must recognize that the amount medical research has received is less than the annual cost of inflation across Canada. Bearing in mind that the cost of medical research-this could be well documented-increases at the rate of 15 per cent to 17 per cent a year in relation to the general rate of inflation which is now in double-digit numbers, there has been a steady erosion in the funding of medical research in Canada.
Let me put this in practical terms. What has this erosion meant to medical research in Canada? Perhaps members in the House know that there are two types of applications: there are requests for renewal of projects and there are requests for funds to support brand new projects. During the past two years, the approval rate for renewed grant requests has risen steadily, to the extent that less and less money for new projects is allocated. What we have found in 1977 is that 7.5 per cent of established or ongoing projects which were considered worthy of continued support had to be terminated and 25.5 per
January 25, 1979

cent of the applications to fund new research projects that have been considered worthy of support were turned down or rejected because money was not available. Those figures had increased substantially by 1978 and 1979, to the point where 40 per cent of the new projects, highly qualified and meeting all the standards, were rejected. Indeed, if my memory serves me correctly, 20 per cent of the older projects have been terminated. That is the type of erosion we have seen in Canada.
There is one other small point I would like to make in that regard. A very special research council committee was formed to review applications for the purchase of major items of scientific equipment designed for multiple use in various institutions, and a sizeable number of applications came forward, but not one of them was approved because of inadequacy of funds.
I note, Mr. Speaker, that you are on the verge of rising to indicate to me that my time is nearly up, so let me conclude by saying that I hope I have demonstrated in a graphic way the importance of medical research and that I have made a case to the government on the importance of medical research in Canada. I wanted more time to talk about the minister's new formula. Let me say quite frankly that I do not find that formula to be adequate. I find that in many respects it is misleading and will again erode the dollars which should be going to medical research. But, as I said, I notice that you are on the verge of rising in your place, Mr. Speaker, so let me simply say again that I hope the government has received the message of the importance of medical research, and I look forward with anticipation to hearing the Minister of National Health and Welfare speak in the debate at a later time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter the debate on Bill C-35 fairly late in the evening. I should like to address myself particularly to Part III which deals with the Department of the Environment. This bill deals with the organization of the Government of Canada, and particularly with the division of the present Department of Fisheries and the Environment into a separate department of the environment and a department of fisheries and oceans.
As members of this House are aware, my party supports the creation of a department of fisheries and oceans. Such action is a long overdue acknowledgement of the importance of the fishing industry to Canadians and the Canadian economy. The promise to create such a department was made five years ago on the eve of the 1974 election, but it looks like this time it will become a reality. I am interested primarily in the implications this bill will hold for the future effectiveness of Environment Canada. I am concerned that this bill does not just create a new department, that it signals the dismantling of a i old one. Certainly Environment Canada has not lived up to the expectations generated at its inception back in 1970 when it was proposed as a super ministry with the powers to co-ordinate and consolidate the anti-pollution efforts of various federal departments and agencies. The mandate for the new depart-
Government Organization
ment read as follows in the Speech from the Throne of October 8, 1970:
There will be proposed the establishment of a department to be concerned with the environment and the husbanding of those renewable resources that are a part of and dependent upon it, with a mandate for the protection of the biosphere.
Because of their close relationship at the time, the government argued it was essential fisheries be brought under the direct control of the new ministry. Now with Bill C-35 we are being asked to consider reverting back to two completely separate ministries, somewhat similar to what existed prior to 1970. I would not argue that fisheries should remain a part of Environment Canada. As my colleagues have already demonstrated, the department consistently struck out when it came to managing our renewable marine resources. Incomes in the fishing industry are generally low and unstable, employment is declining, and the plundering of our offshore resources by foreign countries has led to a severe decline in fish stocks. Perhaps with an independent department of fisheries and oceans, the government will do more to exercise its powers in the area of our offshore fisheries, conservation practices, the settling of quotas, and so on.
However, the removal of fisheries and oceans from the direct influence of the Department of the Environment signals another step in the erosion of the power of that department. The department's mandate is "to protect the biosphere", but the only power it exercises according to this bill is the power to set out guidelines and objectives for other government departments. It can make recommendations, but it does not have the power to enforce the co-operation of these other departments.
As set out in today's bill, foremost among the minister's duties is "the preservation and enhancement of the environment". Yet the actual powers to enforce this mandate do not lie with the Department of the Environment; they are exercised by other government departments. For example, the Department of National Health and Welfare is responsible for the administration of the Environmental Contaminants Act. The Department of Transport is responsible for the Canada Shipping Act which gives it the authority to deal with oil spills. The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources is responsible for the Atomic Energy Control Act which sets the regulations for the disposal of nuclear wastes. The Department of Agriculture administers the Pest Control Products Act, and so on. All of these deal with environmental concerns, but where is the Department of the Environment? It is setting guidelines and objectives, but with no power to see that they are met, or that they are enforced with any consistency by various government administration agencies.
In short, what I am saying is that while this department has the mandate "to protect the biosphere" and to preserve and enhance the environment", it does not have the power required to do so. It is entirely dependent upon the co-operation of other departments and agencies. Despite the minister's exhortations to the contrary, this bill underscores the sad fact that the Department of the Environment is a department without any teeth.

January 25, 1979
Government Organization
The main function of what I might call this lame duck Department of the Environment is to establish environmental objectives and standards, and to co-ordinate the actions of other departments in this regard. The minister's duties are indicated in Bill C-35 as follows:
For the purposes of carrying out his duties and functions related to environmental quality, the Minister of the Environment may, by order, with the approval of the governor in council, establish guidelines for use by departments, boards and agencies of the Government of Canada-
Whether these departments, boards and agencies adhere to these guidelines is a matter for some speculation. If past experience with guidelines set out for the improvement of Great Lakes water quality are any indication, there is little reason for optimism. Great Lakes water quality is an area of many overlapping jurisdictions: international, federal, provincial and municipal. It is of particular concern to me as a representative of the constituency of Brant in southern Ontario where we have witnessed the steady decline of the Great Lakes ecosystem. This situation presented one of the first and most pressing challenges to the Department of the Environment. It also provides an opportunity to assess the department's effectiveness in co-ordinating those activities which are necessary to protect the biosphere and enhance the environment. Unfortunately, many of those activities have been less than successful. The recent history of pollution control on the Great Lakes has been one of missed deadlines, ignored guidelines, and inadequate consultations between the various government agencies and departments involved.
It is interesting to note that when the Department of the Environment was created, it was to bring together concern for the quality of the environment and concern for the sound management of our fisheries resources. The department seems to have struck out on both counts as far as the Great Lakes are concerned.
According to a report issued by the General Accounting Office of the United States government as late or as recent as 1977, the fishing industry on the Great Lakes is doomed. At one time, fishing was a major element in the economy of the Great Lakes area. However, since the 1930s the industry has declined by 83 per cent. The report notes that in 1930 there were 5,284 full time and 1,617 part time commercial fishermen in the Great Lakes. In 1977 there were only 137 full time and 1,043 part time commercial fishermen. The primary reasons for the decline noted in the report are poor management of fisheries resources and, most important, contamination of fish by pesticides and other chemicals which find their way into the Great Lakes. The report indicates that with the present situation there is no chance the number of Great Lakes fishermen or the commercial catch will increase. It is a pretty serious situation.
The importance of Great Lakes water quality to the quality of our over-all environment cannot be underestimated. Together with the United States, we share one of the largest bodies of freshwater on earth. Almost half of the Canadian population resides in the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence basin. When the International Joint Commission issued its report in

1970 that Lake Erie and parts of Lake Ontario were dying, there was great cause for concern, possibly even panic. As indicated in the report, Lake Erie was in "an advanced state of eutrophication" and Lake Ontario was approaching a similar state". In addition, it reported a profuse and proliferating growth of aquatic vegetation in the St. Lawrence River. The causes were primarily attributed to uncontrolled discharges of municipal and industrial waste on both sides of the border.
The report was released at roughly the same time as the creation of the Department of the Environment, a situation which gives an interesting insight into the effectiveness of the department. When the original Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement was signed with the United States in 1972, it was clearly up to the federal government to demonstrate leadership on one of this nation's most urgent environmental issues. The responsibility fell to the Department of the Environment. Its duties and powers, as stated in the bill before us, include:
-the enforcement of any rules or regulations made by the International Joint Commission, promulgated pursuant to the treaty between the United States of America and His Majesty, King Edward VII, relating to boundary waters and questions arising between the United States and Canada, so far as they relate to the preservation and enhancement of the quality of the natural environment.
In the original Water Quality Agreement of 1972, target dates for substantial improvements in water quality were set for December, 1975. That date has long since quietly passed, and the objectives were not met. The latest report of the International Joint Commission, issued last summer, warns that Canada and the United States are still not catching up with pollution on the lakes. It states water quality is not improving and pollution control measures must be taken more seriously if the process is to be reversed. The recommendations of the report, which cost $20 million, took three years of research and involved more than 300 investigations, must be put into force by government action. However, I question whether the Department of the Environment possesses the power necessary to produce the required results. If so, it has certainly been reluctant to exercise it in the past.
Of course, it is powerless to elicit more co-operation from the U.S. to meet our mutual objectives. Studies have shown Canada is far ahead of the U.S on its municipal sewage treatment projects. We can be proud of the fact that Canada is now treating 99 per cent of the sewage waste dumped into the lakes. Only 68 per cent of the sewage from cities and communities in the U.S. meet treatment standards under the 1972 agreement.
However, we are lagging far behind the United States when it comes to enforcing guidelines for Canadian industrial pollution. The worst Canadian polluters are the pulp and paper companies, although Canadian steel producers also lag far behind American producers. According to a 1978 report by the Great Lakes Water Quality Board, the 24 pulp and paper mills in Ontario produced less than half the total tonnage of their 72 U.S. counterparts, but they discharged more than four times the pollution in the form of phosphorous and micro-organisms which feed on the lake's oxygen supply.
January 25, 1979

The new Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement signed last November will place much stricter limits on the dumping of phosphorous into the Lakes. However, the amount of phosphorous pouring into the Lakes is now far in excess of 1972 guidelines. The new agreement gives no indication that the new guidelines will be any more rigidly enforced. If they are not, there is a good possibility that parts of Lakes Erie and Ontario will be changed back into lifeless swamp water, reversing the progress that has already been made.
Part of the reason our corporate pollution record is poor compared to the U.S. is our unwillingness to put some muscle into the enforcement of water quality guidelines. Too often government enforcement agencies are willing to bend when a company threatens loss of profits or lay-offs. This is not the case in the U.S. In 1977 the U.S. Steel Corporation was fined $4 million for discharging ammonia and phenol into Lake Michigan. By contrast, the biggest fine ever levied in Canada was $64,000 against the American Can Co. of Canada Ltd., for allowing mercury to leak into Lake Superior. That is some contrast.
In short, Canada has been soft on its corporate polluters. In its latest annual report, the International Joint Commission wrote:
One of the primary differences between the United States and Canadian approaches to effluent quality, is that plants in the United States were generally required to achieve compliance by July, 1977. In Canada, the compliance dates vary from plant to plant. Also, the corporate stringency of... control requirements may vary depending on the industrial sector, plant, and pollutant being considered.
The U.S. government has used a system of formal permits setting out the limits that industrial plants are required to meet. The U.S. federal government sets minimum standards, but some states set higher standards on their own.
In Canada, the province's limits are set in consultation with the federal government, and I would argue that it is at this time that the Department of the Environment should urge the provinces to adopt the toughest, most uniform standards possible. As it stands now, the provinces negotiate individual compliance standards with each polluter. These schedules can be, and often are, amended at the discretion of the province, very often under extreme duress by a large corporation.
This lack of rigidity, of uniform standards and of federal guidance is one of the primary reasons we are lagging behind the U.S. when it comes to controlling industrial pollution.
This lack of direction from the Department of Environment is evident in other areas, most notably in its failure to live up to its obligations to co-ordinate the anti-pollution activities of other federal departments. I am thinking particularly at this time of the lack of dialogue or interchange between the Department of the Environment and the Department of Agriculture.
The International Joint Commission has identified farm land use activities as a major contributor to polluting Lake Erie. According to reports, two thirds of the phosphorous in the lake has its source in farm run-off. Agriculture has been singled out as a particularly important pollution factor because
Adjournment Debate
of the increasing use of pesticides and uncontrolled discharges of wastes from livestock and poultry.
I am not blaming farmers directly, but I think it is about time the provincial and federal environmental departments and various farm organizations in Ontario and in the United States got together in an attempt to arrange better farm management in order to prevent further pollution from these pesticides that run off from artificial chemical fertilizers on farms where rivers flow south into Lake Erie from Canada, or north into Lake Erie from the United States.
At the same time, erosion of farm land has increased tenfold in the past 15 years, adding a vast amount of sediment to the lakes and choking streams and harbours. There is so much silt in small harbours such as Port Hope, Port Stanley and Port Burwell, to name only a few, that it is dangerous to pleasure boaters and commercial fishermen, and virtually nothing is being done about that. Yet there is no indication the Department of the Environment has entered into discussion on this problem with the federal Department of Agriculture or its provincial counterparts. The Department of the Environment, in conjunction with other departments, should be developing programs which would assist farmers to 'change their farm management practices. There is also a need for financial assistance to establish measures to deal with sediment and farm run-off control. This is an area where the Department of the Environment should be playing a central co-ordinating role, but it is not.
Something has to be done very soon in order to rectify this very dangerous situation that has developed in the Great Lakes lower basin. When one talks about the quality of fishing in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and offshore in eastern Canada, one should bear in mind an image of all this silt, chemical and human effluent, industrial waste and so on that is literally pouring down from the lower Great Lakes into the St. Lawrence River and, past Montreal where most of that city's human effluent is being discharged into the river, and out into the Gulf of St. Lawrence where it is harming fisheries off the east coast. In conclusion, there is a relationship between pollution in the Great Lakes and the fishing industry on the east coast.
