subtopic: FORESTRY-RESEARCH FUNDING OF FOREST MANAGEMENT INSTITUTE
FORESTRY-RESEARCH FUNDING OF FOREST MANAGEMENT INSTITUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 6, 1978, as reported at page 812 of Hansard, I

January 25, 1979
Adjournment Debate
asked a question of the Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Marchand) concerning a contract which was being negotiated by the Canadian forestry service with the Forest Engineering Research Institute of Canada. I suggested then that the work could have been done by the Forestry Management Institute, one of two forestry institutions in Ottawa, the other one being the Forest Fire Research Institute. Both of these institutions were slated to move to Petawawa after a lay-off of approximately 50 personnel.
The origin of this series of events goes back to the announcement by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on August 1, 1978, of the intent to cut back government expenditures in a very massive way. The then president of the treasury board announced on August 15 that a series of government operations would be closed, including the Forest Research Institute at Petawawa. Very substantial representations were made by my colleague, the hon. member for Renfrew North-Nipissing East (Mr. Hopkins). The effect of his representations was to save the operation at Petawawa, and to bring about the closure of two institutes in Ottawa.
Since that time the minister has pursued a policy not only of relocation of what is left of these operations, but of privatizing two forest products institutes, one in Ottawa and the other in Vancouver. The minister confirmed in yesterday's Hansard at page 2515 that there exists an interim chairman of a board which has taken on the job of raising enough money from the private sector, which together with a government grant of some $4 million, will permit these two operations to continue.
My concern relates to the way in which this rather sad series of events unfolded. I support the decision of the government to cut back its budget and to adopt a policy of restraint because it is called for under the present circumstances. However, I cannot help but feel that it would have been better if the policy had been worked through more extensively in private before public announcements were made. Before an announcement is made the proposal should be carefully examined, with all its implications, to prevent changes after the initial public announcement.
I know that the employees of these forest products operations will accept the moves with the best grace possible, but I am concerned about those who terminate their employment with the public service, even if there is an offer forthcoming of private employment. A change of employer is not an easy thing. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) has indicated that all agreements which are in existence will be honoured on behalf of those employees who are being transferred to the private sector. This involves changes which are not easily compensated for. For example, those who subscribe to the public service superannuation benefit scheme and who subsequently move to the private sector will find that there will be some pension adjustment. In many cases the benefits in the private sector are not equal to those in the public service.
I feel that the case for research is not being kept in sight, considering what is actually happening. The forest industry is responsible for something like $7.5 billion worth of exports, as the minister stated when his estimates were before the House.
The contributions of a number of dedicated scientists in this particular industry cannot be underestimated. When the minister assumed his portfolio he addressed a national meeting of foresters and made an inspiring speech, telling them that they had to go out and sell their case for research to the public of Canada. In my public life I have never heard of a stronger case that could be made.
I know every cut is going to hurt. I know the decision on how to cut back is one of the most painful to be made, but I truly believe that the cutback in forestry research will hurt Canadians over the long period. There is a tremendous amount at stake.
I should like to have an assurance from the government that long-term research objectives will continue to be supported when these laboratories are privatized. I should like an assurance that there has been some basic determination of our needs in this area.
At a committee meeting recently I sat with the new Auditor General and we talked about value for money spent. If there ever was a case where value for money could be justified it is in forest research, limited though it has been so far at the federal level.
The people I represent in the national capital region, Mr. Speaker, know that the decision of their employer, the government, has to be accepted and respected. Many members on this side as well as on the other side of the House have raised the question of what the government is doing in this area, and the decisions have now been made. Tonight, I should like to have an assurance from the government that its basic objectives in forest management research will not be neglected.

The decisions and commitments in respect to the FERIC project were made before the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced major reductions in government spending. Inciden-

January 25, 1979

tally, I should like to correct the hon. member's understanding that the Forest Management Institute is to be closed. Rather, it is to be moved to Chalk River where its programs will be amalgamated with those of the Petawawa Forest Experimental Station and the Forest Fire Research Institute.
The Forest Management Institute has some expertise in the renewable energy field. Indeed, these people will act as government project advisers to FERIC and as scientific authorities on other renewable energy projects contracted with the private sector.
To put the matter in perspective, FERIC is not being given funds to conduct forest energy studies at the expense of in-house forest energy research. The funds being contributed to FERIC are part of an expanding government renewable energy initiative shared by the Forest Management Institute and other government establishments. By making better use of the private sector in areas where it has the expertise, we feel this program will benefit the Canadian people and improve Canada's technological capability.

subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-CO-ORDINATOR TO ENSURE MAXIMUM USE OF RAIL CARS TO MOVE GRAIN
CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-CO-ORDINATOR TO ENSURE MAXIMUM USE OF RAIL CARS TO MOVE GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I raised a question with the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board toward the end of December. I asked in effect would the government consider introducing the position of a grain transportation co-ordinator to help co-ordinate and straighten out the mess that we have in grain transportation in Canada. His answer was very unclear at that time, to say the least, and his actions since that time have not led me to believe that a grain transportation co-ordinator for this very vital industry is any closer.
I submit this evening that a grain transportation co-ordinator will help straighten out the transportation mess we have. Grain is not reaching the port of Vancouver in sufficient quantities. And when the port of Thunder Bay was open, it was not reaching that port. This situation was demonstrated by the number of waiting ships, especially at the present time in the port of Vancouver.
Demurrage last year was high. It was in the vicinity of some $25 million, and it will be high again for this coming year. An interesting sidelight that may force some action on this whole question is the fact that within about three weeks the Chinese will be coming to Canada to take the grain that was purchased in the past crop year. They are expecting some 17 ships to load this grain in Vancouver. The unfortunate situation arising at the present time is the fact that the grain is not available. As a result, farmers and people in this country incur large demurrage charges. We have had lost sales in the past year in the order of some $450 million. This has been admitted now by the Canadian Wheat Board. That comes to approximately $3,000 per permit holder.
Under the terms of reference of a transportation co-ordinator I feel that the co-ordinator should have the power over the railways, the unions, the grain companies, the elevator compa-
Adjournment Debate
nies, in effect all facets of the grain industry. The position of a co-ordinator should be brought in and legislated here in the House of Commons. The grain co-ordinator should be responsible to the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board who is in effect responsible to parliament. A person holding this position of grain transportation co-ordinator should hold it for two years. In other words, it should not be a permanent position. We do not want this kind of control over an industry to be permanent in nature. The situation is so serious at the present time that the ultimate or arbitrary power proposed for this individual is necessary for the immediate future.
It is interesting to note that the grain companies are in favour of a transportation co-ordinator, as are some other segments of the grain industry. I feel that this step should be taken immediately. If it is, all parties in the house should give it speedy passage. The time has come for this form of absolute power over the grain industry.
Losses to the farmer and losses to Canada itself in terms of the amount of money grain generates are too great. A grain co-ordinator could be of some help in a labour dispute, if one were to arise at any of our major grain ports. The office of the co-ordinator which I envisage, existed back in the early 1950s. I believe it should be in Winnipeg. The co-ordinator would only need a very small staff because he would have power from parliament. As I mentioned before, his terms of reference should be no longer than two years, and until we get the transportation mess in this country sorted out.
In my opinion the situation has reached a critical stage. The government has studied the industry to death and has not done anything of a positive nature to help it. As an example the situation in Manitoba is very critical in the context that grain has not been moving in this particular crop year and farmers are very short of ready cash. The farmers deserve something better in the way of grain sales than they are getting at the present time. I see no other way than to bring in legislation for a grain transportation co-ordinator and give him the necessary power to straighten out the grain mess in Canada today.

speakeroldname: Miss Aideen Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-CO-ORDINATOR TO ENSURE MAXIMUM USE OF RAIL CARS TO MOVE GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the hon. member's proposal for a grain transportation co-ordinator. This has been discussed in numerous fora. It was discussed briefly at the senior transportation committee meeting on December 13, 1978, and again at the federal-provincial conference of grain handling and transportation on January 8 and 9, 1979.
The general opinion at these meetings was that the setting up of such a co-ordinator is not the best solution to the problem at this time and that a more desirable approach to ensuring that the maximum use is made of our grain handling and transportation capacity is to foster the utmost co-operation between the various segments of the system. The various participants are each experts in their own areas and it is important to make the most efficient use possible of this expertise.

January 25, 1979
Adjournment Debate
If it were to be shown that the appointment of an outside co-ordinator is desirable, that step would be taken. In 1969, with the increased volumes of grain moving into Thunder Bay and Vancouver, it was determined that a grain movement co-ordinator was desirable in order to prevent congestion and unnecessary delays.
Obviously, a co-ordinator who was knowledgeable in the fundamentals of railroading and with some authority was needed. Two co-ordinators were appointed to co-ordinate the efforts of the various segments of port operations toward improving the throughput of existing facilities. They work in close liaison with the local supervisors of the various segments of port operations improving the flow of information and assisting in the resolution of operating problems.
The grain car co-ordinators have performed a vital function in assisting the movement of grain through Thunder Bay and Vancouver. Grain handling innovations have been introduced which probably would not have been possible without the important control function of the co-ordinator. Car unloading levels, rail car utilization and terminal elevator handlings have increased since these co-ordinators were put in place.
While these co-ordinators were necessary and are performing admirably, it does not follow that the co-ordinating function should be extended from the ports to cover the whole system. The system involves interaction between many groups, and over-all co-ordination would be extremely complex. It is desirable to encourage a co-operative approach, as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is doing through the senior transportation committee, and reserve the co-ordination as a position of last resort.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-CIVIL AVIATION INSPECTORS WITHOUT CONTRACT
AIR TRANSPORT-CIVIL AVIATION INSPECTORS WITHOUT CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 19 last, in a motion under Standing Order 43 I drew the attention of the House to the deteriorating situation in civil aviation standards in Canada. My motion requested the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) to put their heads together in order to solve the very serious deteriorating situation with our civil aviation inspectors group.
On December 20, just before the Christmas recess, in the absence of the President of the Treasury Board I asked the Minister of Transport whether he was aware that comparability did not exist for that group with military pilots and air traffic controllers, let alone comparability with the private sector. In a rather offhand manner, the minister pointed out there had been difficulties and disputes involving the collective bargaining process. However, he shared my view that this is a very important group indeed.
The minister did not reply to my request asking him which of three crises he would wait for before something in a meaningful way was done to correct the deplorable condition that existed in the collective bargaining process. As in too

many disputes today, the manipulation of the collective bargaining process is the root cause of attitudes and situations which affect a group as important as the one of which I am speaking.
I have three pages of chronology here involving some 32 steps since December 15, 1973, and this group has been without a contract since 1975. They submitted themselves to binding arbitration, and the Treasury Board negotiators at that time agreed to binding arbitration. Mr. Justice Hall ruled in their favour, yet the Treasury Board saw fit to appeal the case when it went before the AIB.
These people have fallen well behind the income levels of the military air pilots who serve Canada and the air traffic controllers who, because of their power, can shut down our air transportation system with the snap of a finger.
The civil aviation inspectors of Canada are charged with the responsibility of enforcing the law and maintaining a high and desirable standard of civil aviation safety. Their duties are many and varied. They look after more than 21,500 registered aircraft in Canada. There are 83,000 or more personal licences and permits which they supervise. There are licenced air carriers numbering something like 1,360. There are 950 licenced airports and 604 navigational aid systems which need their continuous supervision.
What has happened with this lack of comparability with their counterparts in the civil service, and most certainly with their counterparts out in the industry, is that they have lost spirit and are leaving their service. There are 369 man-years charged to this responsibility, and as I understand it now, over 60 of these have left that service and gone to the private sector.
The tragedy here is that this is a group which has a high standard of education and experience. They are the people who sit behind our commercial airline pilots and approve their performance and their knowledge of their aircraft. These gentlemen have 10,000 flying hours of experience, an average age of 49, and an average of 27 years of aviation experience.
I will give the particular case of one with 19,000 flying hours. He is paid a base of $18,620. He can get flying pay of another $2,400, for a total of $21,000. He is the gentleman who is supposed to rule on the ability of a young pilot flying a Cessna aircraft on the B.C. coast for about a six-month period during the open weather season. This young pilot can make up to $28,000 in six months. The whole flying industry is just laughing at the plight and the condition of these civil aviation inspectors.
I am quite frustrated when I see a government which is supposed to be responsible in this area, and a Minister of Labour who today answered my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), to the effect that it is strange to him that the hon. member would suggest that it is the principle of comparability which is at stake. I was quite shocked at the put-down given by the minister to my colleague, because I know the minister to be a serious and concerned
January 25, 1979

individual. I suggest that he take a very serious look at this very serious situation and the lack of fairness with this civil aviation inspector group within the air operations group of the Department of Transport.
These people are not union-oriented. Their job is to enforce the law. They were told by the Treasury Board that negotiations would begin again on January 3. For some magic reason-part of this game again-negotiations were not proceeded with, and the inspectors went out on strike. Because of a technicality and their respect for the law, they went back to work. Then they were told that there will be negotiations on January 29, but I want to leave the message with the ministers responsible that unless there is a meaningful offer on January 29, I can see nothing but deterioration with regard to this important group, and it is not the type of group which can be put back together once it has disintegrated.
Why is this government insisting on an attitude of destruction and unfairness in the comparability of wage even with their own colleagues in the civil service let alone in comparison with the people they have had to supervise and on whom they have had to enforce the regulations?
I would be very disappointed if the minister replied to me by saying this has anything to do with restraint. There are all kinds of areas where restraint can be applied and there are all kinds of waste in management by this government, but restraint in areas as vital and important to civil aviation in Canada and standards of civil aviation is deplorable, and I urge all three ministers to get to work on this urgent problem.

speakeroldname: Miss Aideen Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-CIVIL AVIATION INSPECTORS WITHOUT CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to provide the hon. member with some additional facts surrounding the aircraft operations group withdrawal of service. At this time the government is seeking clarification from the Public Service Staff Relations Board, through an application process, requesting that the PSSRB declare whether the group is in a legal strike position. This group is responsible for piloting of aircraft as well as inspection and regulation of aircraft equipment and aviation facilities.
There are three subgroups involved. They are: the 356 civil aviation inspectors earning an average salary of $24,854; 17 executive pilots and supervisors whose average salary is
Adjournment Debate
$31,426, and the helicopter pilots and supervisors who number 51 and earn an average income of $25,732.
This brings the total number of employees in the aircraft operations group to 424. The average salary for the group is $25,240. In addition, the civil aviation inspector is eligible to receive up to $2,400 annually as a flying allowance.
The former bargaining agent for the group, the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada, was decertified in July of last year. The Canadian Union of Professional and Technical Employees obtained the bargaining rights.
The group has been without a collective agreement since July, 1975. Both the former and current bargaining agents refused to enter into a new collective agreement. They thought it might prejudice their attempts to have overturned the order of the Administrator, under the Anti-Inflation Act, which restricted the compensation increases to the group to $2,400 annually, the maximum permissible increase under the AIB. This restriction applies to the two-year period from July, 1975, to July, 1977.
However, the government unilaterally implemented the maximum permissible increase under AIB in August, 1976, for the period concerned. This resulted in rates of pay being increased for the group by 11.5 per cent, effective July, 1975, and 9.86 per cent effective July, 1976.
The former and current bargaining agents have refused to sign a collective agreement incorporating these increases as the matter was before the courts. However, in November, 1978, the Federal Court of Canada rejected the challenge made by the bargaining agent.
On December 1, 1978, the government unilaterally implemented the maximum permissible increases under the AIB for the third guideline year giving the group a 9.41 per cent increase to rates of pay effective July, 1977.
As a result, for the period July, 1975, to July, 1978, the average salary for the group has gone up by 38.23 per cent, so that the current average salary is $6,756 higher than in June, 1975. On December 1 last, the government also served notice to bargain for the period beginning July, 1978, which is to start next Tuesday, January 30.
